chunks.text: Chapter 1 The $200-a-Month Mistake It's late on a Tuesday. The shop is closed, the day is finally quiet, and you're on the couch doing the hour of phone admin you resent. You open the bank app to check that a supplier payment cleared, and there it is, sitting between the flour invoice and the card fees: $49. That writing tool. You signed up during a brutal week (a catering quote due, a counter shift to cover, an ad promising "marketing copy in seconds") and you told yourself it was just for now. That was five months ago. It has billed every month since. You have opened it twice. If that sting is familiar, you are in the most crowded club in small business. When Maria Rosey audited the software stack at Viral Nest, the PR firm she founded, she found five tools doing the same job.

"You sign up for a tool during a busy week," she told Forbes in 2026, "you tell yourself it's just for now, then you forget it's even running." Your version might be one $20 line (the graveyard starts at one line) or it might be the full shelf: a writing tool at $49, an SEO tool at $89, an automation plan at $30, a scheduling seat at $10, an AI assistant at $20. That is $198 a month, $2,376 a year. (This invoice is a plausible example, not an average; the shape is what owners keep finding on their own statements.) This book calls it the subscription graveyard. The tools in it are not bad. They are homeless: no recurring task, no person responsible, no number that says whether they help. The mistake is not buying software. It is paying for AI without ever deciding what it is for. Smart, careful people make it every day, and it costs more than money.

Every dead tool was bought with the same hope: that something would finally hand you back an evening. I'll go first. My shelf holds ElevenLabs, an AI voice studio, at five dollars a month. I signed up certain I'd need it. That was about half a year and thirty dollars ago, and I have yet to generate one second of audio. Five dollars a month is exactly how they get you — too small to cancel, too dead to matter, billed forever. After this chapter, you will be able to Find the charges on your own statement that stopped earning their keep months ago Explain why careful owners — you included — end up paying for software nobody uses Run a one-minute test on any AI pitch before it gets near your card Complete a Keep / Prove / Exit audit of every tool you pay for, after watching one done first Protect yourself from tools that die young and from AI your team already uses without asking

Why careful owners collect dead subscriptions Fear signs up. The headlines say most businesses already use AI, and a directory now lists some 47,400 tools to feel behind about. No independent body reviews any of them. The numbers are softer than they look. When BDC, Canada's bank for entrepreneurs, asked owners whether they used AI, 39% said yes. Shown examples first, 66% said yes. The answer depends on the question. And when statistics agencies count businesses actually running AI in their operations, they find 8.8% in the United States and 19.2% in Canada (US Census, 2025; Statistics Canada, 2026). You are not behind. The feeling that you are is manufactured, and it is profitable. The calendar keeps. Rosey named the mechanism: the busy week. Novelty and a deadline start the trial; auto-renewal converts "just for now" into a default. Cancelling requires a decision.

Renewing requires nothing. Vendors understand that asymmetry, which is why trials collect a card number first. Guilt defends. By month three, the tool has cost setup hours and real dollars. Cancelling feels like admitting the waste, so "we should really use it more" becomes the plan. And because no one owns the tool, no one ever has to deliver a verdict. Keeping it feels thrifty; it is the only option that costs money every single month. Economists call this the sunk-cost trap. The graveyard runs on it. Fear signs up, the calendar keeps, guilt defends. That is the whole machine, and every part of it stops the moment a tool has a task, an owner, and a number. You install those three in the next ten minutes of reading. The Noise Test Before believing any tool's promise, including the ones in this book, ask one question: Who profits from me believing I need this now?

Usually: the vendor, an affiliate earning a commission, an investor who needs growth, or a creator whose business is reviewing tools. The product may still be good. But the urgency belongs to the seller, not to you. Then demand four names: Name the task. "Marketing" is not a task. "Turn Friday's customer question into Monday's email" is a task. Name the owner. Who runs and checks it every week? In a one-person business, that is you, which is why the tool count stays small. Name the proof. One result (hours saved, calls answered, bookings made) and a review date in the calendar from day one. Name the exit. How you export your work, cancel, and keep operating without it. Can't name all four? Then do the task manually once and buy nothing yet; a boring manual run shows exactly what software must beat.

Chapter 3 expands these four names into a five-question filter for anything that survives them. Verdict math: $138 a month walks out the door — $1,656 a year back in yours. $30 stays and earns. $30 gets a 30-day deadline instead of another year of guilt. Notice why each tool died. The writing tool fell to overlap: a wide, cheap generalist covers it, which is why a specialist must earn its seat after the $20 tool fails at something valuable. The SEO tool fell to a missing task. Nothing fell to being "bad software." Before cancelling anything, protect the exit: export your work, and check whether a form, calendar, or customer message runs through the tool. Expect the cancel screen to fight back: a 50%-off retention offer, a warning that your data will be deleted. That is the graveyard defending itself. Export first, decline twice. Then cancel on evidence, not guilt.

And this is not theoretical bookkeeping: Amber de la Garza, a small-business productivity coach, says one two-hour audit found her $5,129 in cancelled subscriptions, downgrades, and renegotiated contracts, by her own account on her own podcast; she didn't publish how much of it recurs yearly. Her audit ran long because she renegotiated on the spot. Yours, below, just sorts and totals — the exits can wait for Saturday. A cheap tool without a weekly job is expensive. Two risks worth ten minutes Tools die young. AI tools are mostly young companies running on borrowed money, and young companies fold, pivot, and get acquired; one hobbyist tracker has logged 92 confirmed shutdowns, and nobody counts the full toll. The insurance costs a few dollars: month-to-month billing usually runs higher than the annual plan, by vendor design — for any tool under a year old, pay the difference anyway.

It is the cheapest insurance in this book. Export your data quarterly, and never let one tool be the only place customer information lives. Chapter 3 prices exits properly. Your team is already using AI. MIT researchers found in 2025 that in more than 90% of companies studied, employees used personal AI accounts at work. Ask your people what they already paste into free chatbots (customer emails? the price list?) because nobody vetted where that text goes. The answer closes a data hole and hands you a free list of tools worth piloting on purpose. Chapter 12 turns this into a one-page policy. Do This Friday Total time: about 45 minutes, in pieces. Can't wait for Friday? Do step 1 tonight — it's five minutes, and the bank app is already in your hand. Pull three months of charges (5 min). Search your business card and bank statements for software and app-store payments. Cancel nothing yet.

Build a one-page list (15 min). For each tool: monthly cost, its one task, its owner, the last date it produced something useful. Mark each line (10 min). Keep means task, owner, and proof are all present. Prove means unsure. Exit means no task or no owner. Protect the exits (10 min). Export data, check what breaks, then cancel — through the retention offers, twice. If a tool touches customers, payments, or your website, schedule the safe exit rather than rushing it. Set one proof test (5 min). Each Prove tool gets 30 days, one measurable result, and a calendar date. No new tools during the test. Total the stack (2 min). Multiply monthly charges by 12, then post the total where you will see it before the next free trial. What you just bought back Run the audit and you own something rare: a statement you can explain, line by line, before it arrives.

If your shelf looks anything like this chapter's, you also freed real money: $138 a month is $1,656 a year, about a month of a part-timer's wages. You bought it with 45 minutes and zero new software, and the couch hour goes back to being yours. You'll run the rest of this book the same way, one function at a time, with real prices and the catch always stated. But before you buy anything new, there's a problem: the tools you'll evaluate can lie to you — fluently, confidently, and in perfect grammar. Chapter 2 shows you exactly when to trust AI and when it's bluffing, because the next mistake on the menu is more expensive than $200 a month. The takeaway: do not pay for AI because it is impressive; pay only when a named task, a named owner, and a number prove it belongs in your business.

chunks.text: Chapter 10 Probation: The Rollout You would never defend hiring a person, skipping the trial period, putting them on every job at once, and checking on them "eventually." That is exactly how most AI tools get adopted: bought in an optimistic hour, pointed at everything, reviewed never. This chapter installs the missing employment practice: every tool starts on probation. One job, one metric measured against a baseline, firing criteria written before day one, and a weekly check-in that outlives the honeymoon. The standard unit is thirty days; customer-facing work and agents earn trust on stricter clocks below. The evidence for why comes from businesses much bigger than yours, and it should be read exactly at its labeled size.

Start at home: a Canadian survey of business leaders found 93% of organizations "using AI in some form" and only 2% seeing ROI (KPMG Canada, 2025; the sample skews large). MIT's much-quoted finding points the same way: 95% of formal enterprise AI pilots showed zero measurable return about six months on, under a narrow bar (deployed beyond pilot with measurable KPIs), an enterprise sample, and no small-business breakdown at all (MIT NANDA, 2025). S&P Global found AI-initiative abandonment at 42% of companies, with nearly half of proofs-of-concept scrapped before production (n=1,006, enterprise-wide, 2025). None of these is a statistic about your shop. The protected shorthand ‘pilots fail where nobody owns the follow-through’ is this book's craft warning, not a finding from those studies; none proves why a pilot failed.

So assign follow-through to a person, then test whether that ownership, metric, and deadline prevent drift in your shop. The two questions, run on adoption itself This chapter's delegation isn't a task; it's a change to how work flows. So Chapter 1's two questions (can you check it at a glance, and could you survive the worst version?) bend slightly. Glance-checkable? Only if you baselined: a rollout with no before-number produces vibes, and vibes always favor the tool you just paid for. Survivable? A failed pilot is survivable by design if it was contained: one workflow, real checks, a written exit. It stops being survivable when three tools roll out at once and the failure can't be attributed, or when "we'll see how it goes" runs eight months on autopay.

Bluevine's 2026 small-business survey (n=942, fielded July 2026; a small-business lender polling its own market, so label that too) found 78% of owners don't fully trust AI unsupervised. This chapter reads that distrust as the right instinct and builds it a schedule: supervision designed in, then trusted. After this chapter, you can: Sketch a probation card in five minutes, then prove its exit path before any data or live work enters Baseline a workflow in one week without new software Run the 30-minute weekly review that catches drift while it's cheap End each applicable probation phase with a written decision — never "we'll see" The primary build: the probation card and the weekly review The card (index card, note, whiteboard corner; one per tool, written BEFORE the trial starts): JOB: the one workflow this tool owns during probation. One. ("Answer after-hours calls and book them."

Not "improve operations.") METRIC + BASELINE: the single number that says it's working, its denominator and eligibility rule, and a comparable prior period from your own records. Missed calls booked, quotes sent same-day, evening admin minutes. Predeclare the improvement large enough to matter and the minimum sample that could show it. If you can't name those, you're not ready to hire; run Chapter 7's audit first. CHECKS: which named check from your failure map (Chapter 2's list of how machine work goes wrong, and the check for each) runs on its output, who runs it, and when. (A check that means listening to customer calls has a gate first: the tool announces recording in a way your state's or province's consent rule accepts.) During probation the cadence is doubled: what will be weekly forever is twice-weekly for 30 days.

Sampling is the quality check, not the safety net: a job where a missed call is a gas smell or a burst pipe keeps a real-time human path (Chapter 4's urgent flag and emergency line) regardless of what the sample says. KILL CRITERIA: written now, while you're sober: "Gone unless [rate or margin, with its denominator] beats a comparable baseline by [your meaningful number] after [minimum eligible observations], while staying below [maximum recoverable error or complaint rate], with zero red-line safety, privacy, legal, or irreversible incidents." One red-line incident means immediate containment and firing. The redesign-and-retry rule applies only to recoverable defects. If the minimum sample is too sparse by day 30, EXTEND ONCE is the inconclusive result; if the second window is still too sparse to establish the threshold, FIRE — do not hire on hope.

Chapter 3's pilot rule, now with teeth. EXIT PATH: Probation you can't end isn't probation. Before data goes in, confirm the export and rehearse restore/import where the tool supports it and the state matters. Otherwise open, count, and sample the export, then rehearse a clean-account reconstruction from shop-held prompts, templates, facts, settings, and credential records. Also confirm the connected-system and credential inventory, one-action disable or rollback, manual fallback, authoritative-state reconciliation, retention/deletion handling, cancellation terms, and named owner sign-off. The five-minute card names this work; it does not prove it. Here is one card filled in, a labeled illustration with round numbers, so yours has a model: JOB: answer after-hours calls (introducing itself as an assistant), book them into the calendar.

METRIC: qualified after-hours booking rate; BASELINE: 2 of 11 eligible calls in the comparable prior period, from the call log. MINIMUM SAMPLE: 20 calls under the same eligibility rule; if day 30 arrives before 20, extend once, and if the second window is still sparse, fire. CHECKS: Monday and Thursday, listen to three ordinary calls against the script; independently reconcile every incoming attempt, abandonment, emergency, complaint, refund, requested transfer, and failed handoff against phone, calendar, complaint, and transfer records under the cleared consent flow. KILL: gone unless the qualified booking rate beats 2/11 by my prewritten meaningful margin, while recoverable error and complaint rates stay below my ceiling, with zero red-line incidents and zero invented prices surviving a check.

EXIT: spreadsheet export restore-tested; diversion to the staffed fallback tested; connections and credentials listed for removal; records reconciled from the last good run; deletion/retention and monthly cancellation confirmed; named owner signs off. Every field has a number, denominator, or name; that is the whole trick. Which clock applies? The card is universal. The clock is not. Use the riskiest row that touches the workflow; a hybrid inherits the stricter clock. Workflow class Before controlled live Controlled-live probation Final decision Narrow internal deterministic mutation; no customer send Applicable live-data, failure, fallback, rollback, and exit gates; at least ten clean shadow events across the predeclared window 30 days Day 30: HIRE / EXTEND ONCE / FIRE Frozen outbound customer template, or deterministic receptionist speech or booking

Full watched month in draft, manual, or shadow mode after all gates pass; the system proposes or logs while a person handles the real customer Separate 30 days under the same card and controls End of live phase (normally day 60 overall): HIRE / EXTEND ONCE / FIRE Free-form classification that selects only a frozen customer response or slot Full watched month of classification in draft/manual mode after all gates pass; no generated wording Separate 30 days under the same card and controls End of live phase (normally day 60 overall): HIRE / EXTEND ONCE / FIRE Generated or paraphrased customer wording Draft or human handoff only No autonomous promotion No autonomous HIRE Agent: multi-step planning or action Start with one read-only job on copies; least privilege; tested stop, backup, and rollback

60 days; day 30 is a no-promotion midpoint; weekly run-log review; no unsupervised customer contact or money movement; each send, delete, edit, purchase, or other outside effect requires human approval for that action Day 60: HIRE / EXTEND ONCE / FIRE for the exact tested scope; per-action approval continues, and any new action or permission restarts the gate and 60-day clock For a customer-facing watched month, "shadow" means the system proposes or logs the exact frozen response, slot, or action while a person still handles the real interaction. Promotion after that month is permission to begin controlled live work, not a hire. For an agent, a human-approved outside effect tests only that exact action; it never grants standing autonomy or a wider permission. A card is filed for Chapter 13 only after the applicable row reaches its final decision.

The weekly probation-card review (30 minutes, same slot, non-negotiable during any probation; only this card/metric meeting shrinks to monthly for tenured tools. Workflow checks keep the weekly, real-time, or every-event cadence their own chapter requires): Metric vs. baseline (5 min). Read the number, write it on the card. Check the checks (10 min): confirm the named checks actually ran and re-read their notes (the honest question is "did I skip Thursday?"); no third sampling session, the week's two already happened. Errors and near-misses (10 min): one red-line safety, privacy, legal, or irreversible incident triggers immediate containment and firing. A recoverable defect that survived a check contains the affected workflow immediately and sends the task back while the check gets redesigned.

That redesign consumes the one extension and gets a fixed end date; failure to pass by that date, or a repeat past the redesigned check, fires the tool. For a bad price or promise already delivered, identify every affected customer, deliver the decided remedy, reconcile any money, and record evidence of closure the same day. An attempted callback is not closure. One decision (5 min): continue, adjust the script/instructions (Chapter 2, shape 5: corrections go in writing), or invoke the kill criteria early. Write it on the card. Every applicable phase ends with a written decision. For a narrow internal workflow, day 30 is Hire / Extend once / Fire. For a customer-send workflow, the watched month's first decision is Promote to controlled live send / Extend once / Fire; promotion is not Hire, and a separate 30-day live phase follows.

For an agent, day 30 is a midpoint, not a final decision; day 60 is Hire / Extend once / Fire. Hire: the applicable final phase is complete, the metric cleared, and checks held; the tool joins the payroll, the card/metric review drops to monthly, every workflow-specific check keeps its chapter-defined cadence, and the card gets filed for Chapter 13's audits. Extend once: genuine externalities ate the phase or a recoverable redesign is underway; one extension, fixed new end date, same criteria, no paused fourth state; a second extension is a fire wearing a bathrobe. Fire: criteria missed; cancel this week, per the card's exit path, and write one line about why on the card before filing it. That line is your growing private database of what doesn't work in your shop, worth more than any review site. One workflow at a time is the rule that makes all of it legible.

Two tools on probation simultaneously is the maximum, and only if their workflows don't touch; three is how you end up unable to say which change moved the number. The measured claim, yours as always: a probation costs you the card sketch (five minutes to write, ten if you're deciding the numbers as you go), a separate pre-live block long enough to verify the exit and data gates, the baseline (usually free: last month's number off your own records, a week of counting only when no record exists), four-to-five weekly reviews (about two to two and a half hours total), and the doubled check cadence for the month: your named check, run twice a week instead of once, priced at whatever it costs you. That last line belongs on the tag.

Price all of it against the subscription's annual cost times the years it survives unused on autopay, and the ritual funds itself the first time it fires something. The take-backs, named The big-bang rollout. Everything-at-once adoption makes failures harder to attribute and unwind; this book therefore limits rollout to one workflow at a time. The book's whole sequence (Chapters 4→9) is already in rollout order for a reason. The unbaselined pilot. No before-number, no trial. A tool that can't be measured can't be fired, and unfireable workers run the shop (Chapter 1's owner-who-can't-fire line, now as procedure). "Set and forget." The drift Chapter 9 documented (supervision decaying as fit breeds trust) is the failure mode of successful pilots. The weekly-then-monthly review is not paranoia; it is the price on the tag. A tool good enough to keep is important enough to check.

chunks.text: Chapter 11 Headcount, Honestly There is a question under every chapter of this book that polite business writing tiptoes around, and you deserve it answered in the open: is this thing coming for jobs — mine, or my people's? This chapter answers with the evidence we actually have, in both directions, labeled. It will not promise you that nothing changes. It will also not sell you efficiency dressed up as inevitability. What it owes you is the truth at your size, and the truth at your size is more specific, and more workable, than the headlines in either direction. Both directions, told straight The cut happened, and this book won't pretend otherwise. Sonora, an online guitar school, went from 48 staff to 30.

Among the eliminated roles the reporting names: a dozen appointment setters and a sales manager, as custom AI agents took over scheduling, document handling, and parts of sales, for about $250,000 a year in savings, with results the founder called "slightly better," his words, no metric named in the reporting (TIME, May 2026; independent reporting). Read the labels before you generalize: 48 staff is about five times this book's upper bound, the replaced roles were single-task by design (setters), and the system was custom-built, not bought. Sonora is what it looks like when a mid-size company deletes a layer of identical, delegable tasks that had been hired as jobs. It is a real story. It is not a prophecy about your shop.

Now the other direction, from bigger samples, with their own labels attached: 82% of AI-adopting small businesses grew their workforce (US Chamber of Commerce, 2025), and 56% of small businesses say AI helps them offset headcount challenges (Verizon/Morning Consult, 2025). Both are industry surveys of self-reported experience, run by bodies with a stake in the sunny reading, and growing businesses adopt more of everything, so the arrow between AI and growth is not proven in either direction; read them as directional, the same grade as the worker-sentiment number below. The 56%, in this book's own reading of the survey-speak, mostly means we couldn't hire anyway, and the work still got done. That is the pattern this book has been documenting since Chapter 1: the pizza owner in Chapter 9 employs more people than before the AI took his phones.

At 1–10 staff, the arithmetic runs opposite to Sonora's: you don't usually employ a layer of identical tasks. You employ Maria, who does eleven things, four of which are floor-work. The machine can take those four. It cannot take Maria's ceiling-work (the pricing call with a difficult regular) or her glue (she is the one who hears when a good customer sounds off), and those were the reason you hired her, and a five-person shop that cuts one person loses 20% of its hands, while the machine can cover only the floor-work slice of what walked out. At your size, the machine is capacity you couldn't afford to hire, not a person you get to stop paying. That sentence states this book's operating design, not a forecast or a claim that micro-business jobs are immune from substitution; the evidence above does not establish that.

So here is the book's position, stated once and kept everywhere: this book helps you do more with the people you have and delay the hire you weren't ready for. It does not, and will not, coach you to cut people, and any tool sold to you on payroll elimination at your size should be read as Sonora-scale marketing aimed at the wrong buyer. After this chapter, you can: Answer the jobs question for your own shop with a task map instead of a headline Run the role redesign: floor-work to the machine, people moved up to the work that needs a person Say the true thing to your team, once, in words that survive contact with their worry Face the solo-professional version honestly: when the machine unbundles what you bill The task map: how the question actually resolves Jobs are bundles. The machine takes tasks.

Every honest answer to "will AI replace X" starts by unbundling X, which is Chapter 1's two questions (can you check it at a glance, and could you survive the worst version?) applied to a payroll instead of a to-do list. Sit down with each role in your shop (yours included) and sort its week into three piles: floor-work (repetitive, glance-checkable: the retyping, the drafting, the scheduling ping-pong), ceiling-work (judgment, relationships, the trade skill itself), and the glue (the stuff nobody wrote down: noticing the customer's tone, catching the wrong part before it ships). The machine bids on pile one only. The redesign that follows is the actual answer to the jobs question. The floor-work moves to the machine under named checks. The person's week refills with ceiling-work and glue: the parts of the job that were always the point.

And the checking itself becomes part of their job description: Chapter 2's checks need owners, and a person who runs the checks on machine work has moved up, not out. Name the transition honestly when you hand it over: the first weeks of checking machine work can feel like proofreading a stranger, and a person allowed to say so out loud settles into the new shape faster. That is what "capacity" means concretely: the same payroll, pointed higher, while the hire you were dreading gets deferred until growth, not drowning, demands it. What this requires of you is the honesty to do the redesign with people, not to them.

Which brings in the number that should shape how you speak: in a June 2026 online panel, 35.5% of 1,000 US working adults agreed or strongly agreed that working harder won't protect them from layoffs or AI (Founder Reports; cross-sectional self-report, not small-business staff specifically). Your team was not polled, but if the country's working adults are any guide, someone on your crew may already be quietly braced. Silence reads as confirmation. So map the roles first (all of them, even at five minutes a role), then say the true thing, once, plainly, and early (a role that maps to nearly all floor-work gets its own one-to-one conversation before any group meeting, which is why the fast pass over every role comes before the speech). One version, in this book's words (yours will be better): "I'm using AI for repetitive work — drafts, retyping, scheduling.

This rollout is designed to increase capacity, and no reduction is currently planned because of it. Your jobs will tilt toward the parts that need a person, and checking the machine's work is going to be part of how we all work now. If plans change, you'll hear it from me first, directly and lawfully, not from a tool announcement." Say it your way and keep it to present intent and the truth you can support; future business conditions are not yours to guarantee. Finish the fast pass first, so you are not speaking blind, and have a local employment adviser review any job-security assurance before you give it. Being caught managing your people by stealth costs more than any of Chapter 12's legal trouble, but so does a promise you had no authority to make. The solo professional's version, faced

One kind of reader gets a harder deal here, and this book's own review process (a designed, simulated test reader, not a human one) flagged it early, so it gets answered on the page. If you are a solo professional whose invoices bill floor-work by the hour, this section is yours: the bookkeeper whose real product is the catch but whose line items say ledger-tidying, the VA whose judgment hides inside "inbox management," the freelancer whose work is invoiced as formatting. For you this book's instrument cuts both ways: the same two questions that free an owner's evenings tell your clients which parts of your invoice a machine can draft. For you, "capacity" and "pay cut" can be the same number. No cheerful reframe fixes that, so here is the working answer instead, in rising order of ambition.

Reprice what's already true: move from hours to fixed or value pricing before your clients do the unbundling math for you; you were never selling minutes, you were selling the fact that it's right, and Chapter 1's whole argument is that the checking is the scarce thing: bill for the verification, the judgment, the liability you carry, and let the machine eat the minutes inside a price that no longer advertises them. Move up the stack deliberately: the same trust that let you touch their books opens the advisory work above the books, within what you're licensed and insured to give; floor-work was the door, not the house. And use the capacity as capacity: more clients at the new price, not fewer hours at the old one. What doesn't work is pretending: your most organized clients are reading books like this one.

The professionals who lose the unbundling race are the ones who let the client discover the machine first. The take-backs, named Nobody's whole job. The unit of delegation is the task, never the person. The day a role's entire week fits in pile one, the honest conversation is about redesigning the role, and you have it with the person, with time, like an owner and not like a memo. The quiet cut. "We just won't replace people as they leave, the AI will absorb it" without an actual task redesign is service decay on a delay timer. If attrition changes your shape, redesign on purpose, out loud. (And name this for what it is: the one way headcount ever falls under this book's position — never pushed, sometimes not backfilled, always redesigned in the open.) Can't-verify work, regardless of payroll pressure. A tight month does not repeal Chapter 1.

The tasks behind the line (the filings, the rules you can't judge, the promises) stay with people and professionals even when the machine is free and the payroll isn't. The morale-blind rollout. Announcing tools without the speech above, or worse, letting the team discover them. That braced third is listening to what you don't say. Do this Friday About 60 minutes for one role: 20 to map, 20 to draft the redesign, 15 to draft or adapt the talk, and five for the charter. Additional roles, the live shop conversation, adviser time, lead time, and fees are separate and jurisdiction-dependent; schedule and price them before making an assurance. Map one role in full (20 min), starting with your own: three piles, honest minutes per week on each; the back of an order pad between jobs counts.

Circle the floor-work the machine already handles: the drafting, replying, scheduling, capture, and retyping this book's middle chapters delegate. Schedule each additional role for a later five-minute screen; if a screen finds a week that is nearly all floor-work, that role gets its own full map and one-to-one before any group talk. Draft the redesign (20 min) for that role: which tasks move, which checks the person now owns, what refills the hours. One page. Keep the pages as you work through the roles, same test, same way, with task-based reasons in writing. Before implementing any material change to duties, pay, hours, location, monitoring, employment status, accommodations, or expectations, consult the employee and have a qualified local employment adviser review the contract, human-rights and accommodation, wage and overtime, training, and notice implications.

Document the task-based reasons consistently. Draft the talk at the legal gate (15 min). Before delivery, have a qualified local employment adviser review any job-security assurance and any material role change. If that review is not available yet, use only present-tense facts and make no job-security promise. Then schedule the room or one-to-one conversation (solo? use this slot for step 4), take questions, and let "I don't know yet, and you'll hear it from me first" remain an honest answer. Solo professionals: start pricing your three most common engagements as fixed instead of hourly. Use last year's real hours as starting evidence, then price the full delivery cost: billable and non-billable administration, checking and rework, software, variability and risk buffer, and target profit. Define inclusions, exclusions, and the change-order or out-of-scope price.

Friday's slot picks the engagements and ropes off the time; the real math is its own sitting this week, an hour or more with last year's numbers. You don't have to send the new prices yet. You do have to know them. Write the charter line (5 min) where you'll see it: "Capacity, not cuts. Tasks, not people. They hear it from me first." The takeaway: at your size the machine is capacity you couldn't hire, not a person to stop paying — unbundle roles into tasks, move your people up to the work that needs a person, tell them the truth early, and if you sell hours of floor-work yourself, reprice before the market unbundles you.

Sit down with each role in your shop (yours included) and sort its week into three piles: floor-work (repetitive, glance-checkable: the retyping, the drafting, the scheduling ping-pong), ceiling-work (judgment, relationships, the trade skill itself), and the glue (the stuff nobody wrote down: noticing the customer's tone, catching the wrong part before it ships).
The machine bids on pile one only.
The redesign that follows is the actual answer to the jobs question.
The floor-work moves to the machine under named checks.
The person's week refills with ceiling-work and glue: the parts of the job that were always the point.
And the checking itself becomes part of their job description: Chapter 2's checks need owners, and a person who runs the checks on machine work has moved up, not out.

Name the transition honestly when you hand it over: the first weeks of checking machine work can feel like proofreading a stranger, and a person allowed to say so out loud settles into the new shape faster.
That is what "capacity" means concretely: the same payroll, pointed higher, while the hire you were dreading gets deferred until growth, not drowning, demands it.
What this requires of you is the honesty to do the redesign with people, not to them.

Which brings in the number that should shape how you speak: in a June 2026 online panel, 35.5% of 1,000 US working adults agreed or strongly agreed that working harder won't protect them from layoffs or AI (Founder Reports; cross-sectional self-report, not small-business staff specifically).
Your team was not polled, but if the country's working adults are any guide, someone on your crew may already be quietly braced.
Silence reads as confirmation.

So map the roles first (all of them, even at five minutes a role), then say the true thing, once, plainly, and early (a role that maps to nearly all floor-work gets its own one-to-one conversation before any group meeting, which is why the fast pass over every role comes before the speech).
One version, in this book's words (yours will be better): "I'm using AI for repetitive work — drafts, retyping, scheduling.
This rollout is designed to increase capacity, and no reduction is currently planned because of it.

The solo professional's version, faced
One kind of reader gets a harder deal here, and this book's own review process (a designed, simulated test reader, not a human one) flagged it early, so it gets answered on the page.

The take-backs, named
Nobody's whole job.
The unit of delegation is the task, never the person.

(And name this for what it is: the one way headcount ever falls under this book's position — never pushed, sometimes not backfilled, always redesigned in the open.)
Can't-verify work, regardless of payroll pressure.
A tight month does not repeal Chapter 1.

The morale-blind rollout.
Announcing tools without the speech above, or worse, letting the team discover them.
That braced third is listening to what you don't say.
Do this Friday
About 60 minutes for one role: 20 to map, 20 to draft the redesign, 15 to draft or adapt the talk, and five for the charter.
Additional roles, the live shop conversation, adviser time, lead time, and fees are separate and jurisdiction-dependent; schedule and price them before making an assurance.
Map one role in full (20 min), starting with your own: three piles, honest minutes per week on each; the back of an order pad between jobs counts.
Circle the floor-work the machine already handles: the drafting, replying, scheduling, capture, and retyping this book's middle chapters delegate.

Draft the redesign (20 min) for that role: which tasks move, which checks the person now owns, what refills the hours.
One page.
Keep the pages as you work through the roles, same test, same way, with task-based reasons in writing.

Document the task-based reasons consistently.
Draft the talk at the legal gate (15 min).
Before delivery, have a qualified local employment adviser review any job-security assurance and any material role change.
If that review is not available yet, use only present-tense facts and make no job-security promise.
Then schedule the room or one-to-one conversation (solo?
use this slot for step 4), take questions, and let "I don't know yet, and you'll hear it from me first" remain an honest answer.

Use last year's real hours as starting evidence, then price the full delivery cost: billable and non-billable administration, checking and rework, software, variability and risk buffer, and target profit.
Define inclusions, exclusions, and the change-order or out-of-scope price.
Friday's slot picks the engagements and ropes off the time; the real math is its own sitting this week, an hour or more with last year's numbers.
You don't have to send the new prices yet.
You do have to know them.

Tasks, not people.
They hear it from me first."

Every chapter since has been hiring: a phone answerer, a drafter, a notetaker, a courier. Which means your business now runs a second payroll, the software payroll, and it has the one property no human payroll could survive: workers who never show up keep getting paid, forever, quietly, by card. This chapter is the payroll audit, run on a manager's cadence. It exists because the pattern is universal enough to have a trade name. Maria Rosey, a PR firm founder, audited her stack and found redundant tools accumulating unnoticed.

Her diagnosis is the whole mechanism in one sentence: "You sign up for a tool during a busy week, you tell yourself it's just for now, then you forget it's even running" (a Forbes contributor piece, Aug 2026; the trade calls it SaaS creep). Amber de la Garza, a small-business productivity coach, reports finding $5,129 in a two-hour subscription audit. That's her own account, on her own podcast, so grade it as a practitioner's story, not a study. The vendor-side numbers point the same way, with two labels on them: they come from subscription-management companies, who profit from you believing this. And they measure the small and mid-sized companies those vendors serve, which run bigger than ten people. Read their headline figures (a quarter to thirty percent of spend wasted; roughly a third of seats unused) as directional for your scale, nothing more.

You don't need any of those numbers to be precise. You need one statement sweep to learn your own. After this chapter, you can: Run the quarterly software-payroll audit: every tool lands in Keep, Prove, or Exit Read your card statement in yearly numbers, the only honest unit for small subscriptions Cap "keeping up with AI" at two calendar hours a quarter without falling behind Spot a FOMO ad as Chapter 3's who-profits question in costume, and let it pass without buying The primary build: the quarterly review and triage (about two hours, four times a year) Step 1, the sweep (35 min). Pull thirteen months of every business card and bank account, or a verified recurring-payment report that covers the same window. Add PayPal and other wallets, app stores, cloud marketplaces, vendor invoices, accounts payable, and employee reimbursements.

That is how annual plans and alternate payment channels make the list instead of hiding outside a three-month window. Every software line goes on the list, and every monthly price gets multiplied by twelve in the margin, because $19/mo is noise and $228/yr is a decision. (The author's $5 ghost employee is $60/yr; small numbers are how they get you, which is why the yearly column is the audit's only non-negotiable.) A line you can't identify in ten seconds gets a flag, not a detour: keep sweeping, chase the coded descriptors after, and don't let one mystery charge eat the sweep. Step 2, the verdicts (40 min). Every line gets exactly one: KEEP. It has a probation card on file (Chapter 10), its metric still clears, its checks still run.

Any tool touching live people or business data also needs a current Appendix B clearance whose every row is PASS or justified N/A for the exact tool, plan, account, and workflow. At the first audit, a tool with no card is PROVE, even if you cannot imagine the shop without it: preserve service continuity while it runs the applicable Chapter 10 clock. Historical records may support immediate promotion only when they fill every card field and prove that exact workflow's applicable final phase, metric, and checks all cleared—and, where live data is involved, the exact current Appendix B record is PASS or justified N/A on every row. Watched drafts do not prove a customer-send workflow's separate controlled-live phase; generic historical activity does not prove an agent's day-60 decision. Those phases cannot be shortcut. Without exact proof, keep the tool in Prove under the correct clock.

If clearance is missing or uncertain, contain new live-data intake and run Chapter 12's incident process for data entered before clearance. Billing hygiene lives here too: downgrade any annual-renewing Keep for which you bought more than you need. Follow Chapter 3's rule and stay month-to-month for the first year; after that, compare the annual saving in writing against lock-in and exit risk before prepaying. Keeps are boring, and boring is the goal. PROVE. You feel it's useful but there's no card and no number, or it is a tool whose metric no longer clears. It gets a card today (or an updated one) and the applicable Chapter 10 re-probation with real kill criteria. Feelings don't make payroll; numbers do. A tool you can't name the job of in one sentence starts here at best, and falls straight through to Exit if it also fails the number and opened-it-lately tests.

A tool that worked once (say, a transcription tool added during a busy March): the feeling is real, the card isn't. Card today, every review date for the correct clock on the calendar. EXIT. No job, no number, no opened-it-lately. Three checks before the click, because canceling is the verdict you can't undo: export anything you'd miss (customer records, invoices, history); identify the owner, active users, connected systems, recent API or activity logs, and any downstream job; and read the renewal terms, because some annual contracts want written notice 30 to 60 days ahead and an in-app cancel doesn't count. A cheap connector may never be opened and still move booking data every night, so an uncleared dependency stays in Prove. If the tool held client data, Chapter 12's fence applies on the way out: confirm the vendor's deletion terms, not just your export.

Follow contract terms, provide required written notice, complete the in-app cancellation flow where applicable, and calendar the effective deadline. Expect the vendor to fight the leaving harder than it sold the joining: the discount offer, the guilt screen. An Exit by the audit's own rules, and if the author hesitates over five dollars, the hesitation is data there too. And one more column, for any tool that touches customer or client data, whatever its verdict: has its data page changed since you last read it? Retention, training, sharing.

(First audit: read it once and date the reading; every audit after compares against that date.) A changed answer moves even a Keep to Prove, because the tool you audited is not the tool it just became. Tools changed this quarter; the page has to have met them.

That's it. The FOMO engine (every "the businesses that adopt X this quarter will bury the ones that don't" ad) is Chapter 3's who-profits question answering itself: anxiety is the product, and the subscription is the treatment being sold. You are not behind. You are audited, which is different, and rarer. It is the thing this book has been building since the first evening: an owner whose tools have jobs, checks, cards, and firing dates is done keeping up, because there is nothing to keep up with except her own numbers.

Test restore/import where the tool supports it and the state matters; otherwise rehearse a clean-account reconstruction from shop-held prompts, templates, facts, settings, and credential records. Store a protected backup and have the named owner sign off.

An export button is not an exit path until the result has survived the applicable checks. The take-backs, named Daily AI trend news. Unsubscribe from launch feeds and FOMO roundups. Keep vendor security, privacy, billing, service-status and shutdown notices, plus alerts from your regulator, insurer, accountant, and trade association; those can demand action today. A product trend worth buying can wait for the quarterly audit and a track record. An operational warning cannot. Mid-quarter impulse hires. A new tool between audits needs a probation card before the trial, per Chapter 10, or it waits for the audit. The sketch takes five to ten minutes; its exit and data fields still require separate verification before launch. The graveyard is built from tools that skipped both during a busy week (Rosey's sentence, laminated). Annual prepay on anything unproven.

The discount is the vendor pricing your future regret. Stay monthly through the first year; only after that year, a clean current audit, and a tested exit may annual prepay be considered. The audit skip. Miss a quarter and the payroll grows back; the ritual's whole power is that it's boring, scheduled, and shorter than one vendor webinar. The calendar entry outranks the mood. Do this Friday Friday is the first hour of the audit, not a rushed two-hour cancellation spree. Use 35 minutes to sweep and 25 minutes to begin verdicts; complex exports, cancellations, contract notice, dependency tracing, remaining verdicts, and card work get their own scheduled follow-up blocks. Sweep every payment channel (35 min) across thirteen months (or a verified recurring-payment report with the same reach), list every software line, write the ×12 column. Begin the verdicts (25 min): Keep / Prove / Exit.

Say each tool's one-sentence job out loud; hesitation is data. Stop at the hour and schedule the unfinished rows. For a tool only a teammate uses, get their sentence before you verdict: the dispatcher's answer counts, not your guess at it. Schedule the Exits: reserve a follow-up block with enough time to open, count, and sample the export; test restore/import where supported and material, or rehearse the clean-account reconstruction; back up; and obtain named-owner sign-off before cancellation. In that block, follow contract terms, provide required written notice, complete the in-app cancellation flow where applicable, and calendar the effective deadline. Expect the cancel-flow gauntlet (the discount offer, the guilt screen); your card on file was the product, and leaving is usually the feature they made hardest. Schedule the Proves.

Reserve a separate follow-up block for each Chapter 10 probation card and day-30 review; the five card fields and their exit/data proof do not fit inside Friday's first hour. Calendar next quarter's audit (two hours, thirteen weeks out) and your separate two-hour learning budget. Then close the laptop. That's the whole cadence, and it is genuinely enough. The takeaway: your tools are a payroll — audit it quarterly into Keep, Prove, or Exit with yearly numbers, cap the keeping-up at two hours a quarter, and let the market churn without you; calm is what an audited stack feels like.

chunks.text: Chapter 14 Your Next Twelve Months Thirteen chapters ago you were at the counter after close, wondering whether a machine could do the last job of the day and how you'd know if it did it wrong. You now hold the answers as working equipment: two questions, a failure map, named checks, probation cards, a policy page, an audited payroll. This last chapter is about time: what the next year of this looks like, what changes underneath you, and what doesn't. After this chapter, you can: Place every tool you run on the three-rung ladder and know what check each rung demands Read the four signals of a dying tool and act before the shutdown email Decide switch-versus-sit with one rule: switch on your numbers, sit on the market's Write the one-page plan that turns this book into your next twelve months The ladder: assistant, automations, agents

Machine labor comes in three rungs of independence, and the book has been walking you up them in order. Rung one: the assistant. Work happens when you ask, one task at a time, checked as it lands. The drafting, summarizing, and analysis work in Chapters 4 through 7 lives here. In this book's judgment, most businesses should spend most of their first year on rung one, and a year there is not slow; it is how the checking habits form while the stakes are small. Rung two: automations. Work happens on triggers without your hands (Chapter 8's couriers), but each deterministic trigger, transfer, and fixed-template step follows a recipe you wrote. The failure shape is repetition, the check is the run log, and Chapter 8's promotion rule stands: adversarial tests plus at least ten clean shadow events across the predeclared observation window before a narrow internal mutation may go live.

Customer messaging is stricter: even a frozen approved template stays draft/manual through a full month of watched runs, then begins Chapter 10's separate 30-day controlled-live probation; generated or paraphrased customer language always stays a draft or is handed to a person. Free-form interpretation follows the same two phases before it may autonomously classify intent and select a frozen response or slot. These are the workflow clocks in Chapter 10 and Appendix C. A hybrid workflow is graded by its riskiest component, inheriting rung one's invention and misreading checks as well as rung two's run controls. A transfer bot and an open-ended AI receptionist are not the same hire. Rung three: agents. Software that plans multi-step work on its own: reads the inbox, decides what matters, acts, remembers. This rung is real, and this book's honest report is that at owner scale it is early.

The one documented account found at anything like your size is Scott Bell, a solo bankruptcy lawyer who runs a small fleet of open-source agents on OpenClaw, an open-source agent platform a technical owner hosts and wires up himself. His reported arc reads like a trust ladder: months of specifying "every teensy step," an orchestrator (the agent that tracks what the others did) taking notes, and only then delegated judgment like flagging court notices and drafting reply ideas. Read the label at full strength. The account is a magazine profile, pieced together here from secondhand coverage (NYT Magazine, Jun 2026). Nobody interviewed his clients. Nobody audited an agent's decision. The professional-supervision question never comes up. Read it as a story, not an audit.

And the same platform's public record that season includes an agent reported to have deleted a researcher's inbox, ignoring its stop commands, and another reported to have fabricated figures in board documents (TechCrunch, Feb 2026; Business Insider, Mar 2026). The rung-three verdict by the book's own instrument: agents concentrate exactly what Chapter 1 taught you to price. Wide blast radius, expensive verification. So they inherit the strictest version of every rule, not a waiver. If you climb in year one: one agent, one read-only job on copies; least-privilege credentials; no send, delete, edit, purchase, or other outside effect without approval for that action; a tested stop control; a verified backup and rollback; no money movement or unsupervised customer contact; probation doubled from Chapter 10's standard 30 days to 60; run logs read weekly.

Human approval tests only that exact action, not a wider privilege, and any new action or permission restarts the gate and 60-day clock. If the tool cannot meet that fence, wait. Rungs one and two carry every checkable win this book teaches; your own probation cards will tell you what they returned, and rung three will still be there once it has a track record. One contrast case, for calibrated ambition rather than fever: Base44, launched by a single founder in January 2025, was acquired by Wix that June, five months in, for a reported $80 million upfront (TechCrunch, Jun 2025). The revenue and profit figures along the way were the founder's own, unaudited. The sources document nothing about his verification process, so no moral about "judgment" gets to ride on it. It happened; it is not a plan. The plan is the boring ladder, climbed at the speed of your checks.

Signals a tool is dying, and the switch/sit rule Tools die; a tracker exists just to log AI products that didn't make it. You don't need to predict failures, only to notice the four signals early: The changelog goes quiet: no updates in two quarters while the category moves. Price hikes arrive with nothing attached: monetizing the trapped. Support you once had degrades to a bot with no human path: a vendor that removes its human lane has stopped investing in keeping you. (A tool that was always bot-first gets judged on the other three.) The data-export door narrows: exit risk has increased, whatever the vendor's reason. One hard signal—an export restriction, shutdown notice, security or privacy deterioration, or loss of critical support—triggers an immediate tested export and contingency plan.

Any two softer signals together (a starting rule, not a statute) move the tool to Prove at the next audit. The export runs now, while it still works, because Chapter 9's exit question was always about this day. If the tool held customer data, ask the vendor to confirm in writing what was deleted, when, which backups or legal holds remain, what subprocessors retain, and whether any past model training can be reversed. And for the shinier direction — new tools — the switch/sit rule is: switch on your numbers, sit on the market's. Your probation card's metric sagging, your checks catching more, your audit finding a better-fitting Keep: switch. A launch video, a competitor's ad, a headline about the model that changes everything: sit. Chapter 13 already capped your exposure to the second kind at two hours a quarter; this rule is what those hours are for.

The market will re-run its entire drama annually. Your instrument is built to outlast that churn, because it was never about the tools: two questions, checks that fit failure shapes, probation, a policy page, an audit. None of those names a vendor, which is why a model release can't retire them, and why they, and not a tool list, are what this book asked you to learn. The one-page plan Before any rung-three trial appears on this plan, pass one admission gate: a named operating need cannot be met on rungs one or two, and the relevant lower-rung cards and checks have stayed healthy for at least one clean quarter. Otherwise, stay lower. Write it Friday and review it quarterly. Revise sooner after a failed check, incident, staff or ownership change, vendor-policy change, or new legal or data duty. Five lines:

This quarter's one hire: the single workflow from your pain chapter (the one you flipped to first), on a probation card — Chapter 10's index card: one job, one metric with a baseline, named checks, kill criteria, exit path.

A filled first line reads (labeled illustration): "Q4: after-hours phone answering (it announces itself as an assistant; recording stays off until the documented consent flow is cleared), carded: qualified booking rate vs the call log's baseline; deterministic transfer plus fixed-template intake using approved minimum-necessary fields and pre-approved slots; no diagnosis, negotiation, new promises, or money movement; immediate human escalation outside script; next-morning callbacks confirm the first month's bookings, then Monday-and-Thursday call-listens; gone unless it beats baseline after the prewritten minimum sample, extended once if the month ran too quiet to judge; export path confirmed." The deterministic transfer follows rung two.

Any free-form interpretation or generated customer-facing language inherits the highest applicable controls from Chapters 1, 2, 4, 8, and 10; if open-ended judgment is needed, the workflow must hand off to a human. The standing checks: your named check per delegated task, the weekly review during any probation, the quarterly audit. Three habits; everything else in this book hangs off them. The never-list: your take-backs, written where you'll re-read them: can't-verify work, can't-survive work, money movement, compliance-by-chatbot (those questions go to your accountant or lawyer, not a text box), and whatever your trade adds. The team sentence: Chapter 11's present-intent statement, kept in writing: capacity is the design; no reduction is currently planned because of this rollout; if plans change, they hear it from you first, directly and lawfully.

Next quarter's maybe: the one tool or rung you'll consider then, parked by name, so ads have nothing to sell you in between. The last scene Picture one hypothetical Tuesday, if the checks have held. The phone answers itself politely at 9 p.m. (it identifies itself; any recording runs only under the documented consent flow) and books the job. The quote goes out with a total you re-added in nine seconds. The follow-up sends because it was Tuesday, to a customer who said yes to hearing from you, opt-out line riding along; the books skim clean over one coffee a month, and a reply you drafted-then-humanized to a customer's review brings a stranger to the counter. None of it is dramatic; that was the point all along. Somewhere in there is the evening this book cost you, paid back weekly, and a machine that never became your partner, your oracle, or your replacement.

It became what you hired on page one, once you knew what you were hiring: the strangest employee you'll ever manage, working under the oldest rules you know. Your judgment did this. It was never the thing being replaced. It was the thing being aimed, and it is aimed now. Close the book. The shop is yours, a little more than it was. The takeaway: climb the ladder at the speed of your checks — assistant, then automations, then maybe agents — act immediately on a hard signal, flag two soft signals now for Prove at the next audit, switch on your numbers and sit on the market's, and run the five-line plan; the instrument you built is the part built to last.

chunks.text: Chapter 2 The Worker's Failure Map Chapter 1 left you with two questions (can you check the work at a glance, and could you survive the worst version?). This chapter widens them into four separate decisions, made in order, every time you hand work over. Zeroth, clearance: is this data and this call yours to give a machine at all? For this chapter that gate is categorical: no live customer or employee records, nothing confidential (legal, tax, accounting, health, payment, or anything like them), no authority you don't hold. That whole class of records waits for Chapter 12's controls; until then, pilots run on synthetic data, copies you sanitized yourself, or non-personal business data like inventory, SKUs, menus, and product lists. First, the check: is there a check that runs against reality, and will you actually run it?

Second, survivability: a check reduces risk, it does not remove it, so when yours misses, is what slips through survivable and reversible? Third, the payoff: does the time the task saves beat the time its check costs? Delegate only what passes all four. Those decisions work before you delegate. This chapter is about what happens after: the specific ways the work comes back wrong. Because here is the useful secret about the strangest employee you'll ever hire: its failures are not random. They cluster. They have shapes. And once you can name the shapes, you can name in advance which shape a task invites, the way you know without thinking which jobs the new hire will fumble and which they can't hurt. One warning before the map. A person who is about to fail usually shows it: the pause, the hedge, the "let me get back to you." This worker shows nothing.

Every failure below arrives in the same fluent, organized, confident voice as its best work. The map exists because the voice tells you nothing. The five ways it fails A boundary on the number before the list: five is a starter map, built from documented cases and this book's logged runs, not a census of everything that can go wrong. Shapes 1 through 4 are shapes a task's output takes when it fails; shape 5 is not a task shape at all but a standing rule about the worker itself. And a failure that fits none of them is the map growing, not the map breaking: it becomes a new row with its own check (the Friday exercise shows where to write it). 1. It fills gaps with inventions. When the machine doesn't know something, it can produce something plausible that fits the shape of an answer instead of saying "I don't know" and stopping.

Ask for court cases and it can give you court cases: correctly formatted, persuasively named, and sometimes nonexistent. Amir Mostafavi, a California employment lawyer running his own practice, filed an appeals brief in which 21 of 23 quotations turned out to be fabricated by the AI tools he'd used. The court sanctioned him $10,000, reported at the time as the largest such sanction in the state, and published its opinion as a warning to the profession (Noland v. Land of the Free, September 2025; court record). Note what his story adds to Karlen's from Chapter 1: Karlen was a business owner who couldn't check legal work. Mostafavi is a lawyer. The gap-filling failure got them both, because catching an invented citation requires checking every citation, and the polish gives you no reason to. The tell that isn't there: invented material reads more confident than real material, not less.

The machine is at its most specific exactly where it has the least. 2. It drops things silently. Ask it to summarize, merge, or clean, and the recurring result in this book's logged runs was most of it right and one piece quietly lost. This book ran its own logged trials: six owner-sized tasks, each run past two AI workers, a cheap one and an expensive one, every output checked against the source. The cheap worker's supplier-terms summary dropped one payment condition; its contact-list cleanup merged two duplicates and silently lost a note attached to one of them. No error message. No "I skipped something." The output looks complete because completeness is a look. A person who loses a piece of your paperwork usually knows they lost it.

This worker does not know, which is why the check for this family is a count against the original: count the rows, re-add the total, tick off the clauses, and treat any change you didn't expect as a finding. 3. It misreads with authority. The most dangerous family on this book's map, and the one Chapter 1 made you feel: given a lease clause, the cheap worker explained, fluently and helpfully, that staying on would hand the tenant the exact tenancy arrangement the clause exists to deny. Everything around the error was right, which is what made the error invisible. Misreadings don't look like mistakes; they look like explanations. They cluster where the source material is technical and the reader can't independently judge it: contracts, regulations, tax rules, medical guidance.

New York City ran a version of this experiment at city scale: its official small-business help chatbot told owners they could take a cut of workers' tips and refuse cash, advice the reporting showed was unlawful, the tip-taking under the labor rules protecting workers' tips and the cash refusal under a city rule in force since 2020 (The Markup, March 2024). Official deployment, government branding, confidently wrong about the law it existed to explain. The rule this family teaches: verify against the source of the rule, never against the bot. 4. It leaks its template. The machine has never met your business. When it needs a fact it doesn't have — your company name, your prices, your policy — it will sometimes leave the socket showing: our trials' cheap worker sent back a customer-ready email with "[Your Company Name]" still sitting in it.

This is the least dangerous family because it's the most visible, and it is the reminder the others need: the worker is assembling patterns, not remembering you. Which leads to the fifth shape, the one that owners find hardest to believe. 5. It doesn't stay corrected. This one is different in kind: shapes 1 through 4 are ways a task's output fails, while shape 5 is a standing property of the worker, and it governs every task you delegate. Correct a person Tuesday and they arrive corrected Thursday. Chapter 1 told you why the machine may not: memory features exist, but no vendor claims them as reliable learning from your corrections, and the vendors' own documentation warns the models make things up. So treat every correction as a correction to the draft, never to the worker.

The practical consequence is a habit: anything you find yourself correcting twice goes into your written instructions, the standing prompt, the script, the facts sheet you paste in, because the paper remembers what the worker won't. And if more than one of you types into these tools, the paper must be shared with access control: one facts sheet that the people authorized to use it can reach and no one else, carrying no sensitive data that isn't properly yours to share, one named owner who updates it when a correction repeats, or shape 5 just moves from the machine's memory into each person's separate chat history. After this chapter, you can: Run the four delegation decisions in order (clearance, check, survivability, payoff) before any handoff Name the five failure shapes and say which one a given task invites Match each of your delegated tasks to the check that catches its shape

Explain why "are you sure?" and AI-checking-AI are not verification Write the first rows of your own failure map, with a take-back line The map: task families and the checks that fit them The reason Chapter 1's named checks work is that each one is aimed at a failure shape. Read them as minimum checks: each cuts the risk of its shape, none removes it, and a check can miss, which is what the last column prices. Where a check says compare, it means against the original you hold, knowing what you expected to change; a difference you didn't expect is a finding, not a formatting choice. Here is the whole instrument on one page, built from the six task families in this book's logged trials and the shapes above: Task family The failure it invites The minimum check that cuts the risk If the check fails you Drafts you'll send (replies, emails) template leakage; tone off

read it once before it sends an apology, while the boundary below holds Anything with arithmetic (quotes, invoices) silent omission or slip re-add the total; tick lines against your standard list for the job wrong price to one customer Summaries of documents you hold silent omission tick each item against the original a missed condition surfaces later List and data cleanup silent loss in merges count rows in and out against the merges you expected; re-read each merged entry field by field a lost note, a lost customer Answers from your own facts sheet invention past the sheet's edge check against the sheet; forbid guessing a wrong promise in writing Interpreting rules you can't judge (legal, tax, medical) authoritative misreading none you can run a confident wrong answer you can't detect, which is why it isn't delegated

One boundary on the first row, and it is operational, not a mood: a draft sits in that row only while it involves no money, no commitment or deadline, no complaint or dispute, nothing about an employee, no safety matter, and no personal, confidential, or otherwise sensitive data, and only while one follow-up message could fully take it back. The moment a draft crosses any of those lines (a price, a promise, a policy, a complaint, bulk sending), it leaves the row and takes the facts-sheet row's discipline instead: source attached, numbers recomputed, no guessing past the sheet. The table also sits inside the four decisions, not instead of them: the zero-th gate has cleared the data before any row applies; the check column is the first decision; the last column prices the second; and the third still closes the loop.

A check is work, so cost it like work: when the minimum check for a task costs you more than doing the task yourself, the delegation has failed the payoff decision, and the honest move is to keep the task. Two things about that last row. First, it is not a gap in you; it is the definition of the family (Chapter 1's take-it-back verdict, now with its mechanism attached). Second, the machine still earns a seat beside those tasks: drafting the questions for your lawyer, organizing the documents for your accountant, translating your situation into a clear brief. That is labor pointed at the survivable half of the job. Why you can't outsource the checking to the machine Every owner has the same idea within a week: "I'll just ask it to double-check its own work." Two reasons that fails. The first is mechanical: asking "are you sure?" doesn't consult anything new.

The machine generates a fresh answer in the same fluent voice, and it can just as readily apologize and "correct" a right answer into a wrong one — the confidence doesn't budge either way (a mechanism claim from how these systems work, not a measured rate; our own trials didn't test the are-you-sure flip). The second reason has a court record. Brandon Monk, a Texas attorney, filed AI-generated citations and then used a second AI legal tool to check them. The checker missed the fabrications. The court ordered a $2,000 payment to its registry and required AI education (Gauthier v. Goodyear, November 2024; sanction and order per the court record, the second-tool detail per the case's reporting).

One machine's confident guess does not become verification because a second machine agreed; the lesson of his case is the book's rule: checks run against reality (your documents, your numbers, the source of the rule) or they are not checks. And notice who this book's lawyer stories are about: small firms and solo practices, chosen because they match your scale, not because big firms are immune. The record repeats at that scale. Chong Ke, at a small Vancouver family-law firm, was ordered to personally pay for the time wasted on two invented cases she had filed (CBC, February 2024; the first reported Canadian instance). And one honest note about the pile: its one business owner is Chapter 1's Jonathan Karlen; nearly every other name is a lawyer, not because lawyers are careless, but because courts publish their failures.

Your trade's version doesn't make the paper; it just makes a bad week. That is why this book ran its own logged trials on owner-sized tasks instead of waiting for your case file. Mostafavi, Monk, and Ke are not stupid people. They are busy people in checkable-looking situations where the checking was the whole job, and the polish said it was already done. Your week contains the same trap at smaller stakes, which is the only reason this chapter exists. The Worker's Failure Map
Chapter 1 left you with two questions (can you check the work at a glance, and could you survive the worst version?).
This chapter widens them into four separate decisions, made in order, every time you hand work over.
Zeroth, clearance: is this data and this call yours to give a machine at all?
For this chapter that gate is categorical: no live customer or employee records, nothing confidential (legal, tax, accounting, health, payment, or anything like them), no authority you don't hold.

That whole class of records waits for Chapter 12's controls; until then, pilots run on synthetic data, copies you sanitized yourself, or non-personal business data like inventory, SKUs, menus, and product lists.
First, the check: is there a check that runs against reality, and will you actually run it?
Second, survivability: a check reduces risk, it does not remove it, so when yours misses, is what slips through survivable and reversible?
Third, the payoff: does the time the task saves beat the time its check costs?
Delegate only what passes all four.
Those decisions work before you delegate.
This chapter is about what happens after: the specific ways the work comes back wrong.
Because here is the useful secret about the strangest employee you'll ever hire: its failures are not random.
They cluster.
They have shapes.
And once you can name the shapes, you can name in advance which shape a task invites, the way you know without thinking which jobs the new hire will fumble and which they can't hurt.
One warning before the map.
A person who is about to fail usually shows it: the pause, the hedge, the "let me get back to you."
This worker shows nothing.
Every failure below arrives in the same fluent, organized, confident voice as its best work.
The map exists because the voice tells you nothing.
The five ways it fails
A boundary on the number before the list: five is a starter map, built from documented cases and this book's logged runs, not a census of everything that can go wrong.
Shapes 1 through 4 are shapes a task's output takes when it fails; shape 5 is not a task shape at all but a standing rule about the worker itself.
And a failure that fits none of them is the map growing, not the map breaking: it becomes a new row with its own check (the Friday exercise shows where to write it).
It fills gaps with inventions.
When the machine doesn't know something, it can produce something plausible that fits the shape of an answer instead of saying "I don't know" and stopping.
Ask for court cases and it can give you court cases: correctly formatted, persuasively named, and sometimes nonexistent.
Amir Mostafavi, a California employment lawyer running his own practice, filed an appeals brief in which 21 of 23 quotations turned out to be fabricated by the AI tools he'd used.
The court sanctioned him $10,000, reported at the time as the largest such sanction in the state, and published its opinion as a warning to the profession (Noland v.
Land of the Free, September 2025; court record).

Mostafavi is a lawyer.
The gap-filling failure got them both, because catching an invented citation requires checking every citation, and the polish gives you no reason to.
The tell that isn't there: invented material reads more confident than real material, not less.
The machine is at its most specific exactly where it has the least.
It drops things silently.

This book ran its own logged trials: six owner-sized tasks, each run past two AI workers, a cheap one and an expensive one, every output checked against the source.

No error message.
No "I skipped something."
The output looks complete because completeness is a look.
A person who loses a piece of your paperwork usually knows they lost it.

This worker does not know, which is why the check for this family is a count against the original: count the rows, re-add the total, tick off the clauses, and treat any change you didn't expect as a finding.
It misreads with authority.

Everything around the error was right, which is what made the error invisible.
Misreadings don't look like mistakes; they look like explanations.

Official deployment, government branding, confidently wrong about the law it existed to explain.

It leaks its template.
The machine has never met your business.

It doesn't stay corrected.

Correct a person Tuesday and they arrive corrected Thursday.
