chunks.text: Chapter 3 The Five-Question Filter DoNotPay sold itself as "the world's first robot lawyer." For a subscription, it promised to fight parking tickets, generate legal documents, and let you sue anyone at the press of a button. No law degree, no billable hours, no retainer. For an owner with a dispute worth less than a lawyer's first hour, the pitch lands exactly where it hurts. In September 2024, the Federal Trade Commission announced that DoNotPay had agreed to provide $193,000 in monetary relief and to stop claiming its AI matched a human lawyer unless it could prove it. The FTC's complaint was almost boring. The company had not tested whether its robot lawyer worked at the level of a human attorney. It had not even hired lawyers to check.

The final order, approved unanimously in January 2025, added a separate requirement: DoNotPay had to tell its own past subscribers about the settlement. Notice what the FTC did not say. It did not say AI cannot help with legal paperwork. It said nobody had checked whether this AI could. The product had never been reviewed. The marketing, eventually, was. That enforcement action made DoNotPay one of the most scrutinized AI products in America. The tens of thousands of other tools on the market have faced less scrutiny. There is no Consumer Reports for AI, and the regulator shows up occasionally, after the damage. Nobody is coming to review the tool you are about to buy. So the review has to be yours, and short enough that you will actually run it. This chapter is that review: five questions, one index card, about thirty minutes.

The filter is distilled from three sources that take the problem seriously: the Small Business Administration's vendor checklists, the AI Risk Management Framework from NIST (the federal standards body), and MIT's research on why AI pilots fail. You get the five questions that survive translation into plain English. Think of this as the job interview for Chapter 1's strangest employee, and start with the question that decides whether a candidate even gets the interview. The incentive check: who profits from me believing this? Every claim that reaches you arrived on someone's payroll. The vendor profits if you believe the demo. The affiliate reviewer profits if you click their "honest comparison" (Chapter 5 breaks down the commission rates). The course seller profits if you feel behind.

None of that makes a claim false, but it sets the burden of proof: a paid voice earns belief with evidence, not enthusiasm. Run the incentive check out loud, name who profits, and most of the noise disqualifies itself before the interview starts. Whatever survives gets the five questions. Expect most to fail by question three. That is the filter working. This is not Chapter 1's zero-th data-clearance gate: that gate still runs before you give any tool information or authority. After this chapter, you will be able to Put any AI tool through five questions on an index card in about thirty minutes Price a tool at your real volume (seats, tasks, add-ons, twelve months) instead of its sticker price Spot where a "free" plan actually ends before it traps a working habit Run a ten-minute preliminary screen of a vendor's data practices and exit; never mistake it for live-data clearance

Run the first 30-day decision with one metric and written kill criteria, then use Chapter 10's stricter clock for customer-facing work or agents Question 1: What task, and measured how? A tool that promises to "transform your marketing" is making you do its thinking. Which task? "Send the weekly special to the email list every Thursday" is a task. "Answer the phone when we're closed" is a task. "Marketing" is a department. Then walk the chain to a number, link by link. The tool drafts the Thursday email. The email goes out on time instead of skipping busy weeks. More customers open it. Some order. If every link holds, the tool earns money. If you cannot walk the chain, the benefit is a slogan. MIT's much-quoted pilot research points the same way if you look only at the tools that survived.

The tools that were kept produced a measurable result inside a real workflow, inside a defined window. The merely impressive got dropped. That reading is this book's, not the study's own claim, and the study watched big companies, not shops; Chapter 10 sizes it honestly. Before any trial, write down the current number. How long does Thursday's email take today? How many calls went unanswered last week? A baseline costs five minutes now and settles every argument later. Owners who win with AI talk in numbers. When a Florida news outlet profiled Growbo, a small marketing agency, founder Matt Ackerson could put figures on his AI systems: about 700 hours and $12,000 saved in four months. The figures are his own and the article shows no ledger behind them, so add salt. The point survives the salt: he had numbers because he measured, which is the whole ask of question one.

The rule: a tool you cannot measure is a tool you cannot fire. It will sit in the subscription graveyard drawing $29 a month forever, protected by the vague feeling that it helps, until Chapter 13's audit finds it. Question 2: Who runs it every week? The most common review of small-business software is eight words long: "We should really be using that thing more." Software does not run itself, and AI software especially does not. Someone connects it to the calendar and the inbox. Someone feeds it this week's prices. Someone reads what it wrote before a customer does. In Bluevine's 2026 survey, 78% of small-business owners said they do not fully trust AI to work unsupervised. They are right; Chapter 2 showed the machine lying with perfect confidence. Supervision is not a flaw in the plan. It is the plan. So name the supervisor before you buy. A name and an hour: "Nadia, Friday, 8 to 9."

If the answer is "the team," the answer is nobody. If the answer is you (and in a business your size it usually is), question two has a second half: which hour of your week does this replace? A tool that needs an hour of babysitting must save clearly more than that hour, or it is a hobby with an invoice. Question 3: Where does my data go? Every AI tool is a new place where your business information lives. What goes in is rarely just "text": it is customer names and phone numbers, your prices and margins, the draft policy about the employee problem you asked for help wording. It is probably already happening informally. MIT researchers reported in 2025 that in more than 90% of the companies they studied (big companies again, not shops), employees were using personal AI accounts at work, pasting work material into free consumer chatbots nobody vetted.

Owners have noticed the stakes: 33% named data security as a barrier in Bluevine's 2026 survey, up from 23% the year before. The worry is growing because usage is growing. You do not need a security department. You need three answers, findable on the vendor's own site in ten minutes: Does it train on my data, and is there an off switch? Business plans usually say no or let you opt out; free consumer tiers often say yes, quietly. Can I export everything, and delete everything, if I leave? Which plan is built for business use? The free version and the business version of the same product can carry different privacy terms. Until you have checked, treat a free AI tool like a postcard: write nothing on it you would mind someone else reading. A business plan and a training-off switch are checks, not permission. Default to dummy or sanitized records.

Before live customer data enters, complete Chapter 12 and confirm the minimum fields, purpose and lawful authority or consent; the vendor agreement or data-processing terms; subprocessors; storage and cross-border transfer; security and access; retention and deletion; your notice duties; and the incident process. If any of that is uncertain, get advice for your jurisdiction before connecting real records. Count the business tier and that review in the trial budget. If the tool records or transcribes calls or meetings, one more rule no vendor page will surface: your state or province may require the other person's consent before recording; check that rule before the pilot, not after. Health, financial, and children's information stay out until a qualified professional clears the arrangement, including any agreement the law or your contract requires.

Chapter 12 goes deeper, including one fact-specific, nonbinding tribunal award after an airline chatbot described a discount wrongly. The legal effect of any bot statement depends on the facts and local law; the book's stricter house policy is simpler: treat what your tools say as something your business may have to answer for. Question 4: What does it cost at real volume? The sticker price is the price of the demo. The real price arrives around month six, and it is set by how software charges: per seat, per task, per "operation," per employee, per resolved ticket. An example with honest math. Intercom's AI support agent was estimated at ~$29 per seat per month, plus ~99 cents for every conversation the AI resolves (August 2026 secondary snapshot; check the vendor's current page). Resolve 300 tickets a month — a good month — and the estimate is roughly $326, not $29.

The tool may still be worth it. But that decision belongs to the current all-in number. Free tiers deserve the same math, because their caps can arrive just as a working habit forms. Treat the cap as part of the price and model your likely volume. Here is where "free" actually stops, as of August 2026. Prices change, so check the vendor's page before you buy. Tool What free really gets you First paid dollar The catch Zapier 100 tasks/mo, two-step automations only Pro ~$29.99/mo Task billing climbs fast as automations multiply Make 1,000 credits/mo (its unit of work), 2 active scenarios Core ~$9/mo A credit is one step, not one finished job n8n Free only if you host it yourself Cloud ~$25/mo Self-hosting is a part-time technical hobby ChatGPT Capable free tier, shifting limits Plus $20/mo Limits and model access change with little notice Otter.ai ~300 transcription minutes/mo

Pro ~$8.33/mo, billed annually The low monthly price requires paying a year up front Calendly One event type ~$10–16/seat/mo Per-seat pricing grows with every hire Run your own numbers the same way: real monthly volume × unit price, plus a seat for everyone who needs one, times twelve. The Five-Question Filter
DoNotPay sold itself as "the world's first robot lawyer."
For a subscription, it promised to fight parking tickets, generate legal documents, and let you sue anyone at the press of a button.
No law degree, no billable hours, no retainer.
For an owner with a dispute worth less than a lawyer's first hour, the pitch lands exactly where it hurts.
In September 2024, the Federal Trade Commission announced that DoNotPay had agreed to provide $193,000 in monetary relief and to stop claiming its AI matched a human lawyer unless it could prove it.
The FTC's complaint was almost boring.
The company had not tested whether its robot lawyer worked at the level of a human attorney.
It had not even hired lawyers to check.
The final order, approved unanimously in January 2025, added a separate requirement: DoNotPay had to tell its own past subscribers about the settlement.
Notice what the FTC did not say.
It did not say AI cannot help with legal paperwork.
It said nobody had checked whether this AI could.
The product had never been reviewed.
The marketing, eventually, was.
That enforcement action made DoNotPay one of the most scrutinized AI products in America.
The tens of thousands of other tools on the market have faced less scrutiny.
There is no Consumer Reports for AI, and the regulator shows up occasionally, after the damage.
Nobody is coming to review the tool you are about to buy.
So the review has to be yours, and short enough that you will actually run it.
This chapter is that review: five questions, one index card, about thirty minutes.

The filter is distilled from three sources that take the problem seriously: the Small Business Administration's vendor checklists, the AI Risk Management Framework from NIST (the federal standards body), and MIT's research on why AI pilots fail.
You get the five questions that survive translation into plain English.
Think of this as the job interview for Chapter 1's strangest employee, and start with the question that decides whether a candidate even gets the interview.
The incentive check: who profits from me believing this?
Every claim that reaches you arrived on someone's payroll.
The vendor profits if you believe the demo.
The affiliate reviewer profits if you click their "honest comparison" (Chapter 5 breaks down the commission rates).
The course seller profits if you feel behind.
None of that makes a claim false, but it sets the burden of proof: a paid voice earns belief with evidence, not enthusiasm.
Run the incentive check out loud, name who profits, and most of the noise disqualifies itself before the interview starts.
Whatever survives gets the five questions.
Expect most to fail by question three.
That is the filter working.
This is not Chapter 1's zero-th data-clearance gate: that gate still runs before you give any tool information or authority.
After this chapter, you will be able to
Put any AI tool through five questions on an index card in about thirty minutes
Price a tool at your real volume (seats, tasks, add-ons, twelve months) instead of its sticker price
Spot where a "free" plan actually ends before it traps a working habit

A tool that promises to "transform your marketing" is making you do its thinking.
Which task?

"Marketing" is a department.

The tool drafts the Thursday email.

More customers open it.
Some order.
If every link holds, the tool earns money.

The merely impressive got dropped.

How long does Thursday's email take today?
How many calls went unanswered last week?

It will sit in the subscription graveyard drawing $29 a month forever, protected by the vague feeling that it helps, until Chapter 13's audit finds it.

Someone connects it to the calendar and the inbox.
Someone feeds it this week's prices.
Someone reads what it wrote before a customer does.

A tool that needs an hour of babysitting must save clearly more than that hour, or it is a hobby with an invoice.

Every AI tool is a new place where your business information lives.

It is probably already happening informally.

The worry is growing because usage is growing.
You do not need a security department.

Does it train on my data, and is there an off switch?
Business plans usually say no or let you opt out; free consumer tiers often say yes, quietly.

A business plan and a training-off switch are checks, not permission.

chunks.text: Chapter 4 Never Miss Another Customer On a Sunday morning last year, a plumbing company booked a $1,060 job while the owner was still in bed. Nobody at Riley Plumbing & Heating answered that call, because nobody was working. An AI phone agent picked up, talked the customer through the problem, checked the schedule, and booked the visit. That story comes from ServiceTitan, the company that sells the tool, so take the shine off it accordingly. But the mechanics are not marketing. The call came in. Something answered. The job got booked. At most small businesses, that same call rings four times, goes to voicemail, and dies there. This chapter is about some of the cheapest revenue you will ever find: the customers already trying to give you money. Run Chapter 1's two questions on this domain and you'll see why a narrow slice goes first.

Routine booking can be checked quickly because every slot lands in your calendar and every call leaves a log. It becomes survivable floor-work only after the system has an emergency stop, prohibited-topic routing, disclosure and consent controls, a staffed human handoff, and a passed pre-live test. Without those fences, a phone line is not low-stakes at all. After this chapter, you will be able to Measure your missed-call leak in dollars per week from your own phone log Decide whether an AI receptionist, booking links, or both fit how your customers reach you Set up the four-step pipeline that makes the money: answer → book → follow up → ask for the review Write the plain-language script an AI answering tool needs before you buy anything

Keep your AI's promises bounded and reviewable: a narrow script, a human handoff, and written decisions after the watched month and the controlled-live probation The leak you're not measuring Here is the uncomfortable math, with its sourcing shown, because these numbers are shakier than the phone-answering industry admits. The only actual measurement we found is a vendor's own: a local-marketing firm monitored the phone lines of 85 small businesses for a month and clocked roughly 62% of calls going unanswered. Nearly four in ten reached voicemail, and a quarter rang into nothing (411 Locals' self-published study; the visible page date and the reported original-study date conflict, so neither is used here; the exact split is in this chapter's source note). Small sample, seller's pen. Treat it as directional.

And the companion statistic every vendor repeats, that 85% of callers who reach voicemail never call back, traces to no study at all. We followed the citations; they run in a circle of vendors quoting each other. What survives without any study is the part you know from your own dialing habits: people don't leave a message. They call the next name on the list. You never know they existed. Put real numbers on it. Say your average job is worth $300, and you close half the people you actually talk to. Every ten missed calls is ten conversations you never had, five jobs you never won, $1,500 that went to a competitor whose phone got answered. That is the ceiling, not the count: subtract the spam, the repeat callers, the ones who tried again, and the current customers who would have reached you anyway. Friday's count of your own log settles it; no one else's multiplier is required.

Run that math across a year and you understand why industry estimates of the annual cost of missed calls for a small service business run from $26,000 to $126,000 depending on the trade. That range is vendor math, so treat it as directional; the per-call arithmetic above, done on your own log, is the number that counts. (If your work is retainer clients rather than inbound quote calls, your leak lives in Chapter 6's quiet threads, not the ring count.) Meanwhile, most owners trying to "do AI" are generating social media posts. Marketing pours water into the top of a leaky bucket. This chapter plugs the hole in the bottom. The order matters: capture the demand you already have before you spend a dollar creating more. Why speed is the whole game

Sales research has repeated one finding for years, and its actual source is older and humbler than the legend: in a 2007 InsideSales.com report (the company sells lead-response software, so it has a stake in the finding) coauthored by then-MIT Sloan faculty fellow James Oldroyd, an observational analysis of more than 15,000 web leads across six companies associated a first call at five minutes with about 21 times the odds of reaching the companies' qualification threshold compared with a first call at 30 minutes; qualification meant entering the sales process, not completing a sale. That association is a reason to test speed, not proof that speed caused revenue. Your own comparable call-log probation decides whether faster answering pays in your shop. You cannot personally be that fast at 7 p.m. on a Tuesday. You are quoting a job, or making dinner, or finally off the clock.

For decades the options were an answering service, a hired dispatcher, or your own interrupted evening. The genuinely new thing AI brings is a fourth option: software that answers every call, instantly, for about the price of one small job a month. Owners who set this up describe the same two results. First, booked work they would have missed. Second, and they mention this almost as often: the phone stops owning them. Dinner is dinner. That second result is why this book keeps insisting AI's best gift to a small business is not head count math. It is getting pieces of your life back: capacity and relief, never a promise about cutting people. What "answering" needs to include An AI receptionist that just takes messages is voicemail with better manners. The setups that make money do four things in a row. Think of it as one pipeline: answer → book → follow up → ask for the review.

Answer every call, 24/7. The AI greets callers, handles the three questions that make up most of your volume (are you open, do you serve my area, what does it roughly cost), and takes details for anything unusual. Book straight into your calendar. Not "someone will call you back." The caller hangs up holding a time slot. G.L. Hunt, a family-owned Texas foundation-repair company, reports a 40% higher booking rate after wiring AI follow-up into its missed-call handling. That number comes from Hatch, its software vendor, so treat it as a best case. The math that matters is smaller and yours: the secondary snapshot below estimated the AI answering tools at ~$79–99 a month, and the honest break-even counts more than the sticker.

Total the current subscription and usage charges, the cost of setup and integration time, and the weekly audit-and-check labour over a stated period (a quarter is fair). The business case is one line: the margin on one booked job your log says you were losing must beat that all-in cost. Follow up automatically. Missed a call anyway? The system texts back within a minute: "Sorry we missed you — want to book a time or tell us what you need?" A text that arrives while the customer is still on your competitor's hold music wins ugly and often.

One law check before the texting goes on, Canada first: a commercial text or email needs a lawful basis you could document, identification of who sent it, and a working unsubscribe; under CASL an inquiry or application can support implied consent for about six months, and a direct response to a request, inquiry, or complaint sits differently again; the sender keeps the proof either way (the CRTC's guidance pages, in the note). A US workflow needs its own current-source or qualified-advice check for the exact channel and purpose; this book does not infer automated-message permission from a missed inbound call. If the posture is uncertain anywhere, the default is a manual callback, not an automated text. Confirm the posture against the source of the rule, never the vendor's FAQ (Chapter 12). Ask for the review. Job done, the system requests a Google review and drafts your reply.

Reviews feed the next customer's decision, which feeds the phone, which is the whole loop. This book's conservative house rule puts an electronic review request through the same lawful-basis, sender-identification, proof, and unsubscribe checks as the follow-up above; exact duties vary by channel and jurisdiction, so confirm yours. If you cannot document the basis and controls, ask manually or put a neutral review link on the receipt. The same house rule sends the ask to everyone or no one—never screen out unhappy customers first—and waits until the job is actually settled, with no open complaint or callback and repeat customers asked at most a few times a year. Confirm the current platform and regulator rules before automating the ask. Restaurants run the same play with orders instead of appointments.

Little Italy, an independent restaurant, put an AI agent on its phone line connected to its Toast register and went live in three days (the vendor, Loman, tells the story, same caveat as above). The vendor's telling leads with a front-of-house labor-cost cut above 24%, which is the exact pitch this book promised not to make. So read that number as proof the phones got covered, not as a payroll plan. Three stories, three vendors' pens, each labeled as it passed: that is the honest state of the public evidence at this scale. And one decoupling before the shopping list: those stories belong to ServiceTitan, Hatch, and Loman, which are not the tools in the table below. The stories show what the category can do; the tools below have prices and trial windows, not published proof, and your 30-day log is what turns a trial into evidence.

The one number in this chapter you can trust outright is the one you pull from your own call log on Friday. The tools, with prices and catches Prices are from August 2026 and change often; check the vendor's page before you buy. Every tool here has a catch, listed, because every tool everywhere does. Tool Price What it is The catch Goodcall ~$79/mo flat AI phone answering, unlimited minutes Setup and calendar integration take real effort up front My AI Front Desk ~$99/mo Phone + text + web chat + booking in one bundle Less customizable than single-purpose tools Calendly free; ~$10–12/seat/mo Booking links that kill phone tag Free plan = one event type; use free/monthly through year one WiserReview free; ~$9–19/mo Review monitoring + AI-drafted replies Free tier covers one location

Industry-specific versions exist and often fit better: Voksha for salons and clinics (~$50–150/mo), Yelp Host for restaurant reservations and phone orders, Jobber's AI features if you're in the trades and already run your business on it. The vertical tool costs more and locks you in; the trade is less setup. Chapter 9 covers that decision properly. One tool to be skeptical of: the website chat widget. The conversion numbers quoted for chat widgets trace back to whole-site benchmarks from other industries, not to chatbots on small-business sites, so this book offers no benchmark; if you ever add one, run it as a Chapter 10 probation (a tryout with a kill date) against your own baseline. If your lead log shows qualified calls dominate, test phone capture first.

Otherwise baseline every channel and fix the largest measured leak; the chat widget earns no automatic priority or automatic one-year delay. Never Miss Another Customer
On a Sunday morning last year, a plumbing company booked a $1,060 job while the owner was still in bed.
Nobody at Riley Plumbing & Heating answered that call, because nobody was working.
An AI phone agent picked up, talked the customer through the problem, checked the schedule, and booked the visit.
That story comes from ServiceTitan, the company that sells the tool, so take the shine off it accordingly.
But the mechanics are not marketing.
The call came in.
Something answered.
The job got booked.
At most small businesses, that same call rings four times, goes to voicemail, and dies there.
This chapter is about some of the cheapest revenue you will ever find: the customers already trying to give you money.
Run Chapter 1's two questions on this domain and you'll see why a narrow slice goes first.
Routine booking can be checked quickly because every slot lands in your calendar and every call leaves a log.
It becomes survivable floor-work only after the system has an emergency stop, prohibited-topic routing, disclosure and consent controls, a staffed human handoff, and a passed pre-live test.

Write the plain-language script an AI answering tool needs before you buy anything

Small sample, seller's pen.
Treat it as directional.

We followed the citations; they run in a circle of vendors quoting each other.
What survives without any study is the part you know from your own dialing habits: people don't leave a message.
They call the next name on the list.
You never know they existed.

This chapter plugs the hole in the bottom.

That association is a reason to test speed, not proof that speed caused revenue.
Your own comparable call-log probation decides whether faster answering pays in your shop.
You cannot personally be that fast at 7 p.m. on a Tuesday.
You are quoting a job, or making dinner, or finally off the clock.

An AI receptionist that just takes messages is voicemail with better manners.

chunks.text: Chapter 5 Marketing Without a Marketing Department Picture the version of you that marketing advice is written for: posts three times a week, runs seasonal campaigns, "engages with the community." Now the real version: your business page last posted eleven weeks ago, the photo was good, and every day since, a small voice has said you should really post something while you did actual work instead. (That scene is an illustration, not a case study. If it stung, it's yours; if not, the loop below is still shorter than whatever you're doing now.) Here is the honest frame for this whole chapter: marketing was never your job, and it became your job anyway. Nobody opens a shop to write captions. But the market moved word-of-mouth onto screens, so the words have to exist.

And this is already the most common job owners hand the machine: in a 1,683-business Canadian survey, content creation was the top use of generative AI, named by 84% of the owners already using it (CFIB, 2025; that is 84% of the survey's 525 generative-AI users). The survey counted content creation broadly; this chapter makes a split the survey doesn't: the words are one thing, and the pictures of what you sell are another. The question was never whether owners would delegate the words. It's whether they delegate them well. Shahezad Contractor runs Cousin's Food Inc., a Philadelphia halal restaurant group that did over $4 million in revenue in 2025.

He uses an AI assistant for social content, training materials, forecasting, and site scouting, and he has explicitly avoided hiring a content writer (CNBC, March 2026; independent reporting, and a size caveat: multi-location, bigger than most readers of this book). Notice the shape of his win, because even at his bigger-than-you scale it is this book's capacity doctrine in one line: the business grew and the content got made and the marketing hire didn't happen. Not jobs cut: a hire deferred, by labor priced at assistant rates ($0–20/mo to start, the class Chapter 8 shops for; his exact stack isn't in the reporting). And before the demo sweeps you: Victoria Savage runs Rustic Rebel Sourdough, a one-person bakery in Capreol, Ontario.

She posted AI-generated teaser images of upcoming sandwiches and caught a public backlash from her own customers; she defended the choice on cost grounds, "every penny counts" (CBC Sudbury, July 2026; independent). One person, one small shop, and the customers still noticed and still minded. Hold both stories. They are the map of this domain: low-stakes words grounded only in facts you supplied are safe to delegate under a check, and the pictures of what you sell are a different thing entirely. What the two questions say about marketing Run Chapter 1's two questions over the marketing pile and something convenient appears: most of this domain is the good kind of delegation. Can you check it at a glance? For words about your own business: yes, better than anyone alive.

A draft post about this week's special, a reply to a positive or routine review, a newsletter paragraph about your new hours. You know instantly whether it's true and whether it sounds like you. The check is one read. Could you survive the worst version? Here marketing splits in two. A slightly generic caption that slips through: survivable, invisible, the cost is mild mediocrity. But marketing is public and permanent, so three specific classes fail the survivability question, and they get their own section below: images that misrepresent what you sell, claims and offers the business has to honor, and anything that trades on being authentically you when it isn't. A complaint, injury or safety allegation, discrimination claim, refund dispute, or legal threat is not routine marketing at all: the machine may organize facts you supply, but a named person owns the response and escalation.

So the domain verdict, up front: delegate the drafting of words grounded in real events of your business, under a one-read check. Keep the camera, the claims, and the taste. After this chapter, you can: Build a one-page Voice Pack that makes every AI marketing draft sound like you Run a 30-minute weekly loop that keeps your channels alive off real events Name the three marketing delegations you never make, and why Choose your stack ($0, ~$30–50, or content-as-strategy) on arithmetic instead of ads The primary build: a Voice Pack and a weekly loop This is the one build this chapter asks of you. No new paid tools required to start; the assistant you already have is enough for the loop itself. Step 1 — the Voice Pack (30 minutes, once). One page, in your words, saved where you can paste it: Who you are and who you serve, in two sentences you'd say out loud.

Five words you'd use; five you never would. (If "elevated" makes you gag, write it down.) Your three standing facts: hours, service area, the thing you're known for. Two public posts or sanitized excerpts you wrote and were proud of, pasted in as voice samples. No customer, employee, health, payment, order, contact, or confidential details. One rule line at the bottom: "Draft only from the facts and events I give you. If you need a fact I didn't give, ask; never invent specials, prices, or claims." That last line is Chapter 2's no-inventing fence doing marketing duty (shape 1: the machine fills gaps with plausible inventions; a written boundary gives your check something to catch them against). The Pack is your standing instruction, because paper remembers what the worker won't. Step 2 — the weekly loop (about 30 minutes of desk work, same day each week).

Bring three real events from the week: a job finished, a product back in stock, a question three customers asked. Strip names, contact details, order facts, and anything confidential before you paste. Paste the Pack, paste the safe facts of the events, ask for drafts. Then the checks, in order: true? (facts against what happened) · yours? (read it aloud; would you say it across the counter?) · promises? (any price, offer, or deadline gets checked like a quote, because it is one). Fix or cut, then schedule the week. (More than one of you posting? The loop still works: "yours?" then means "matches the Pack," and whoever owns the Pack reads the week's drafts once.) Use a real photo where a photo is needed; take it while you're already on site, but count the actual capture, rights or permission, selection, and upload time in your first run.

Before posting, scan every pixel for customers, staff, children, addresses, licence plates, screens, documents, health details, and anything else identifying; crop or redact it, and offer a no-penalty way to stay out of the photo. Worked once (labeled illustration): the event is an oven repair pushing Saturday's bread two hours late; the draft comes back "Bread's late Saturday: oven repair this morning. First loaves out at 11, croissants unaffected, day-olds half price while we catch up." True? That is what happened. Yours? It survives reading aloud. Promises? Half price is a price: recompute it, confirm you'll honor it, post. (That one goes out same-day — late bread can't wait for the schedule; the week's other drafts get scheduled as usual.) The measured claim, in your arithmetic, not mine: count what a posted week costs you now in evenings and avoidance.

The loop's price is roughly half an hour plus the checking discipline. Whether that trade clears is your number; the book promises none. chunks.text: Chapter 6 Follow-Up That Runs Itself Somewhere in your sent folder is a quote from three weeks ago that never got an answer. You meant to follow up. Then Thursday happened, and following up started to feel like pestering, and now it feels like too late. (Labeled illustration, but check your sent folder before you call it hypothetical.) Here are the plain mechanics of the leak: follow-up doesn't die of skill. You know exactly what to say to the customer who went quiet; you'd say it perfectly if they walked in. Follow-up dies of memory and mood: remembering on the right day, and feeling like it isn't begging. Which makes this domain almost comically well-suited to the strangest employee you'll ever hire, because the machine has no Thursday and no pride. It never forgets the day, and it never feels awkward.

What it doesn't know is what you're allowed to promise, which is why the split of labor in this chapter is the cleanest in the book: the calendar and the drafts are the machine's; the promises and the judgment stay yours. Chapter 4 caught the customer who called. This chapter is about everyone who almost bought: the quote unanswered, the "let me think about it," the estimate that went quiet. Before any tool, one piece of honesty from the research: the CRM-failure numbers the industry repeats trace to no study that measured them (the closest real survey measured usage and self-reported impressions, not returns), so this book prints none of them. The pattern the number was invented to describe is still worth naming, as this book's own judgment, and it is the one this chapter is built to avoid: owners buy memory (a CRM) without wiring the habit (the follow-up loop).

The software remembered everything and nobody sent anything. So we build the loop first, on tools you mostly have, and let a CRM earn its way in later, if ever. The two questions, run on the quiet leads Chapter 1's screen for any delegation (can you check it at a glance, and could you survive the worst version?) runs cleanly on the quiet leads. Glance-checkable? A follow-up message is a short draft grounded in facts you hold: what you quoted, when, for what job. You can check it in one read. Yes. Survivable? A follow-up that's slightly stiff: survivable everywhere. Two versions are not survivable, and they draw the domain's lines.

A follow-up that changes the deal (a discount you didn't authorize, a date you can't hit) is a wrong promise in writing; only an introduced or changed price, quantity, date, deadline, guarantee, or commitment is re-added or recomputed, as applicable, by you before it goes anywhere. A copied factual measurement (like a 40-foot run) is source-checked against the quote, not recomputed (Chapter 2's standing rule). And persistence without a stop is reputational: the machine will happily send touch number nine, so the count and the tone ceiling are decisions you make once, in writing, not per-send. After this chapter, you can: Run a two-touch follow-up loop on every quote and quiet lead, drafted for you, sent with your check Decide when a CRM is actually earned (later than the ads say) and which class to buy

Name the follow-up delegations you never make: deal changes, cold blasts, and endless sequences Count your own leak in quotes-without-answers, this Friday, from your sent folder The primary build: the two-touch thread One spreadsheet (or a page in your notes app), one calendar, the assistant you have. Zero new dollars to start. 1. Capture: the thread list. One line per open lead: name, what was quoted, date sent, next-touch date, eligible/not eligible, reply, booked/won/lost, lost reason if known, unsubscribe, and complaint. Ten seconds at the moment you send any quote, then one result mark when the thread ends. This list IS your CRM for now; the discipline of writing the line is the habit every failed CRM purchase was trying to buy. 2. Touch one, day 3: the useful nudge. Not "just checking in."

Until Chapter 12's live-data gate has cleared the drafting tool, build the reusable message with placeholders such as `[FIRST NAME]`, `[JOB DETAIL]`, and `[DATE]`, then fill them locally from the quote and calendar. A sendable shape to copy: "Measured your gutters against the quote from Tuesday — the 40-foot run is why the number looks high. Happy to walk you through it, and next week's install slots are open Thursday and Friday." You read it once against the two checks that matter: is everything in it true, and would you say it across the counter? If the draft introduced or changed any fact you gave it (the measurement, the price, the slot), it goes back for a source check against the quote and the calendar before anything sends.

Before either touch goes live, confirm the lawful basis or consent for that channel, keep the proof, identify the sender, and include the unsubscribe control your rule requires; if you cannot document the basis, do not send. Rules differ by country, so check yours. Send only after those gates pass. 3. Touch two, day 10: the honest close. The machine drafts the version you'd never quite write yourself because it feels too direct: "Wanted to close the loop on the quote from the 4th. If the timing's wrong or you went another way, no hard feelings; if you'd like the slot, I'm holding availability through Friday." Use the same placeholders and channel-compliance gate as touch one. True dates only, per the recompute rule. Send. 4. Stop. Two touches, then the lead moves to a "later" list that gets one seasonal note, ever.

One consent check before that note: a past customer is not permanent permission. The note needs a lawful basis you could document; under Canada's CASL an inquiry or application can support implied consent for about six months, a direct response to a request or complaint sits differently, and windows age out. So the note names who sent it, carries an unsubscribe, the proof of the basis gets kept, and any name you're not sure about gets deferred, not messaged (the CRTC's own guide; rules differ by country, so check yours). That stop is written policy. It protects the asset every follow-up spends a little of: being someone whose messages people open. One exception runs the other way: when what you're chasing is owed to you (the documents, signatures, or statements you need before you can do the work), the two-touch cap comes off.

The reminder repeats on a calendar, polite and unembarrassed, because it isn't selling anything; it's collecting what was promised. Even this lane gets a written edge: weekly, four times, then you pick up the phone, and the machine never sends a fifth. 5. The schedule link. If your business books time, put a scheduling link in both touches. Calendly (free; Standard estimated at ~$12/seat/mo monthly, ~$10/mo billed annually) kills the where-does-this-go ping-pong. The annual figure is comparison only; Chapter 3 keeps you on free or monthly billing through year one. Skip it if jobs need a site visit before any booking is real: a link that books unquotable work manufactures awkward calls. Calendly's estimate was checked Aug 2026 from secondary sources; the current vendor page rules.

The measured claim, yours to compute: count last month's eligible quotes and estimates that got no reply and no follow-up (Friday's step 1 turns this same count into a working list). Multiply that count by your estimated follow-up response rate, then by your historical close rate after a response, then by contribution margin per job, not full revenue. Until your thread list supplies a local response rate, run a low and high scenario and label it an assumption. The result is recoverable contribution margin under the scenario, not the pipeline's face value and not a promise (the "speed-to-lead" folklore stays in Chapter 4 where its sourcing is disclosed).

Automation, when the volume justifies it: the touches above can fire automatically from a form or a missed call (Chapter 8's glue: a two-step automation on the free tiers covers "new row → reminder"; a text-back on a missed call pairs with Chapter 4's stack). One channel note before anything fires as a text: texting is its own legal lane (TCPA in the US, CASL in Canada), so any template that can go out as a text carries an opt-out line, and Chapter 4's law check runs before the switch flips. Automate the reminder and the draft first, keep the send manual until a month of reading drafts has taught you the failure shapes on your own leads. After that month, only a frozen, human-approved lowest-stakes template with approved field substitution may send automatically.

Any generated or paraphrased customer language remains draft-only, and texts stay manual until the consent and opt-out handling is confirmed. When a CRM is actually earned Buy customer-relationship software when, and only when, all three are true: the thread list exceeds what a page can hold (dozens of simultaneous open leads), more than one person works the leads, and you've run the loop manually long enough to know your own stages. (Worked once, as illustration: forty wedding-season inquiries spill past your page, yes; more than one person works the leads, no, it's just you; you know your stages after a season, yes. Two of three is not all three: keep the page.)

Then buy the small class first: Zoho CRM (estimated ~$14/user/mo; big capability per dollar, smaller ecosystem) or HubSpot's free tier (real, but built as a ramp: the paid jump was estimated at ~$100/seat/mo for Sales Hub Professional, so decide at the free ceiling, not after the habits form inside it). Skip both if the thread list still fits on a page; a CRM at that size is a subscription for guilt. Estimates checked Aug 2026 from secondary sources; current vendor pages rule. And the class you likely never buy at 1–10 staff: cold-outreach machinery (contact databases, mass sequencing, deliverability warmup (the slow work of keeping mass email out of spam folders); a category estimate, ~$47–185/mo and up across the class, checked Aug 2026, secondary-sourced; no vendor named on purpose, since this aisle is the take-back). It exists for B2B pipelines with dedicated salespeople.

For a local service business, mass cold email is a reputation tax with legal edges. In Canada, the anti-spam law CASL demands consent you can prove, with penalties that can run into the millions (the CRTC's own guidance carries the current numbers; rules differ by country, so check yours). Every dollar of it is better spent answering the phone (Chapter 4) and following the warm thread (this chapter). And if you are determined to run outbound anyway, that is the day you pay for an hour of real compliance advice, not a forum thread. That's a take-it-back on an entire aisle of the store, and it stands until your business genuinely becomes an outbound B2B operation. The take-backs, named Any follow-up that introduces or changes a price, quantity, date, deadline, guarantee, or commitment.

The machine drafts around them; only an introduced or changed price, quantity, date, deadline, guarantee, or commitment is re-added or recomputed, as applicable. A copied factual measurement such as the 40-foot run is source-checked against the quote, not recomputed. A generated discount is a wrong price published to the one customer you were trying to win. The negotiation itself. When they reply with "can you do it for less?", the machine's job ends at organizing your options. The answer requires judgment about your margin, your season, your read of the person — the half of the job Chapter 1 calls ceiling-work, and it doesn't delegate. Endless sequences and cold blasts. Two touches and a seasonal note, warm leads only. The math of one more automated touch always looks free, and the bill lands somewhere real: every future message's open rate. Buying memory before the habit exists.

The CRM take-back above, kept on paper where next quarter's ad can't argue with it. Do this Friday About 30 minutes, $0. Open the sent folder. Count eligible quotes and estimates from the last 30 days with no reply and no follow-up. Write the number down. Estimate recoverable contribution margin as eligible quiet quotes × expected reply rate × historical wins per reply × contribution margin per job; if your records already give wins per eligible quiet quote, use that direct rate instead. Track eligible, replied, won, lost, and no-reply outcomes under one rule, and use a range where any input is uncertain. Build the thread list from those: name, quote, date, next touch. Five minutes of typing.

Draft both touches once with your assistant, using placeholders until Chapter 12 has cleared live customer data and using your Voice Pack if you've built one (that's Chapter 5's one-pager; starting here, two standing facts plus two phrases you always say do the same job). Save them as templates; fill customer facts locally from the quote and calendar. Send touch one to the three most recent that are at least three days old only after the lawful-basis, proof, sender-identification, and unsubscribe gates above pass for that channel. Automated sends, texts, recording, or review solicitations stay manual/off until official guidance or a qualified local privacy/compliance professional has cleared the exact flow when its classification is uncertain. Somewhere in your sent folder is a quote from three weeks ago that never got an answer.
You meant to follow up.
Then Thursday happened, and following up started to feel like pestering, and now it feels like too late.
(Labeled illustration, but check your sent folder before you call it hypothetical.)
Here are the plain mechanics of the leak: follow-up doesn't die of skill.
You know exactly what to say to the customer who went quiet; you'd say it perfectly if they walked in.
Follow-up dies of memory and mood: remembering on the right day, and feeling like it isn't begging.
Which makes this domain almost comically well-suited to the strangest employee you'll ever hire, because the machine has no Thursday and no pride.
It never forgets the day, and it never feels awkward.

What it doesn't know is what you're allowed to promise, which is why the split of labor in this chapter is the cleanest in the book: the calendar and the drafts are the machine's; the promises and the judgment stay yours.
Chapter 4 caught the customer who called.
This chapter is about everyone who almost bought: the quote unanswered, the "let me think about it," the estimate that went quiet.

Before any tool, one piece of honesty from the research: the CRM-failure numbers the industry repeats trace to no study that measured them (the closest real survey measured usage and self-reported impressions, not returns), so this book prints none of them.

The pattern the number was invented to describe is still worth naming, as this book's own judgment, and it is the one this chapter is built to avoid: owners buy memory (a CRM) without wiring the habit (the follow-up loop).
The software remembered everything and nobody sent anything.
So we build the loop first, on tools you mostly have, and let a CRM earn its way in later, if ever.
The two questions, run on the quiet leads
Chapter 1's screen for any delegation (can you check it at a glance, and could you survive the worst version?)
runs cleanly on the quiet leads.
Glance-checkable?
A follow-up message is a short draft grounded in facts you hold: what you quoted, when, for what job.
You can check it in one read.
Yes.
Survivable?
A follow-up that's slightly stiff: survivable everywhere.
Two versions are not survivable, and they draw the domain's lines.

A follow-up that changes the deal (a discount you didn't authorize, a date you can't hit) is a wrong promise in writing; only an introduced or changed price, quantity, date, deadline, guarantee, or commitment is re-added or recomputed, as applicable, by you before it goes anywhere.
A copied factual measurement (like a 40-foot run) is source-checked against the quote, not recomputed (Chapter 2's standing rule).
And persistence without a stop is reputational: the machine will happily send touch number nine, so the count and the tone ceiling are decisions you make once, in writing, not per-send.

Run a two-touch follow-up loop on every quote and quiet lead, drafted for you, sent with your check
Decide when a CRM is actually earned (later than the ads say) and which class to buy
Name the follow-up delegations you never make: deal changes, cold blasts, and endless sequences
Count your own leak in quotes-without-answers, this Friday, from your sent folder

One spreadsheet (or a page in your notes app), one calendar, the assistant you have.
Zero new dollars to start.
Capture: the thread list.
One line per open lead: name, what was quoted, date sent, next-touch date, eligible/not eligible, reply, booked/won/lost, lost reason if known, unsubscribe, and complaint.
Ten seconds at the moment you send any quote, then one result mark when the thread ends.

Touch one, day 3: the useful nudge.
Not "just checking in."

Until Chapter 12's live-data gate has cleared the drafting tool, build the reusable message with placeholders such as `[FIRST NAME]`, `[JOB DETAIL]`, and `[DATE]`, then fill them locally from the quote and calendar.

The machine drafts the version you'd never quite write yourself because it feels too direct: "Wanted to close the loop on the quote from the 4th.

True dates only, per the recompute rule.

So the note names who sent it, carries an unsubscribe, the proof of the basis gets kept, and any name you're not sure about gets deferred, not messaged (the CRTC's own guide; rules differ by country, so check yours).
That stop is written policy.
It protects the asset every follow-up spends a little of: being someone whose messages people open.

chunks.text: Chapter 7 The Back Office on Autopilot The back office is where your evenings go to die: the receipts in the console, the invoice you'll send "tonight," the meeting you'll definitely remember the details of (you won't), the books you'll catch up on Sunday. None of it is your trade. All of it is your job. And it is the densest concentration of floor-work in your entire week, which makes it the domain where Chapter 1's arithmetic pays best. Josh Chapel runs Mana Accounting, a three-person firm, on an AI bookkeeping platform (Digits); he reports that cleanup jobs that used to eat afternoons now finish in minutes. That account is the owner's own, in a trade publication (CPA Practice Advisor, Oct 2025), so grade it accordingly: a practitioner's report, not an audit. But notice who it comes from: an accountant, delegating accounting floor-work.

The person best equipped to check the machine's bookkeeping is the one leaning on it hardest. One story proves nothing, but the shape it illustrates is this book's whole doctrine: delegate hardest where you can check fastest. The two questions, run on the paperwork pile Chapter 1's screen for any delegation (can you check it at a glance, and could you survive the worst version?) runs cleanly on the paperwork pile. Glance-checkable? Most of the back office, yes, and better than any other domain: a receipt confirms vendor, amount, and date, but not always the right category, tax treatment, or deductible share; a transcribed meeting has your memory of the meeting; a drafted invoice has the job you just did. The source of truth is usually in the room, but ambiguous classifications still need a person who knows the books. Survivable? Split by destination.

Work that stays inside (notes, drafts, categorizations you'll review): worst case is a correction. Work that lands outside (an invoice to a customer, a number in a filing): gets the recompute check, or doesn't go. And one class in this domain has a survivability problem most owners never consider, and it gets its own take-back below: recordings of other people. After this chapter, you can: Run the admin-hours audit and name your two biggest evening-eaters in minutes per week Set up the pair with the fastest payback for most owners per your own audit: meeting notes (checked the same day) and receipt capture (checked monthly) Draw the filing line: what never goes out the door without recomputation Apply the recording fence before the first meeting gets transcribed The primary build: audit first, then the two workhorses Step 1 — the admin-hours audit (15 minutes, once).

List last week's non-trade work in five buckets: money-in (invoices, chasing payments, chasing the documents clients owe you) · money-out (receipts, bills, categorizing) · meetings-and-notes · scheduling · retyping-between-systems. Put honest minutes next to each. Two numbers will embarrass you. Those two are your delegation targets. This chapter builds the two winners the audit most often surfaces, in this book's own judgment (meetings and money-out), and covers money-in below; if your two are scheduling or retyping-between-systems, the builds live in Chapters 4 and 8, but they run under this chapter's checks either way. Step 2 — meeting notes (the fastest win, if you meet). Transcription plus AI summary turns an hour's meeting into searchable notes with action items.

Fathom (free tier covers Zoom, Meet, and Teams with 5 AI summaries a month; ~$19/mo beyond, nearer $15 on annual billing; checked Aug 2026 across several independent roundups, check the current vendor page before buying) or Otter.ai (free ~300 min/mo; Pro ~$8.33/mo billed annually, roughly $100 up front; checked 2026-08-07, check the current vendor page before buying). Chapter 3's first-year rule still governs both tools: use a free tier or monthly billing in year one; consider an annual plan only after that year, a clean current audit, and a tested exit. Pick by where your meetings actually happen: Fathom lives on the video platforms, so if your client meetings are walkthroughs and phone calls, Otter's phone app records in the room (confirm the feature at the vendor page), or type your notes after.

Skip both if your "meetings" are two texts and a phone call: a notetaker for meetings you don't have is a subscription for a fantasy. And one fence before any notetaker joins a real call: a transcript is other people's words in a third party's cloud, so the recording take-back below applies from the FIRST meeting, not eventually. Before the tool joins, say its name, what it records, why, who can access it, the relevant retention/training facts, and that typed notes are the no-penalty alternative; record the yes outside the recording and explain how withdrawal or deletion requests are handled. No answer, hesitation, staff pressure, or uncertainty about the local, contractual, professional, or workplace rule means typed notes instead.

The check: skim the summary against your own memory the same day; the machine's summaries drop things silently (Chapter 2, shape 2), and same-day you still know what mattered. Step 3 — receipt and expense capture (the compounding win). Snap-a-photo capture with AI categorization, inside whatever accounting tool you use: QuickBooks Online (~$30–120/mo; an Aug 2026 price increase was reported, check the current page), Xero (~$25–55/mo), Wave (free core, ~$20/mo add-ons) for bootstrappers, FreshBooks (~$20–50/mo) if invoicing is your center of gravity. All prices secondary-sourced Aug 2026; vendor pages rule. The notetaker's data check applies here too, before any bank feed connects: where the books live, and whether the vendor trains on them. Start with the exact plan you already pay for and verify its current receipt-capture feature page.

Do not switch suites for this chapter: migration is its own project with its own cost, and this book has not established feature parity across these plans. Delegate extraction first. Auto-classify only vendors and categories already approved in your bookkeeping map; mixed-use, capital, unusual, or unclear items go to an exception queue for your bookkeeper or accountant. Once a month, run the captured and categorized list with coffee, reconcile it to the account, and clear the exceptions before anything files. You are not re-doing the work; you are staying able to catch what a receipt alone cannot prove. The day you can't spot a wrong category is the day the books are managing you.

Also worth their line: invoice drafting from job notes (inside the tools above, or your assistant plus your template; recompute every number before send), plus the chasing itself: the payment nudge and the document reminder (the papers clients owe you) run as reusable drafts on Chapter 6's follow-up loop, pointed at paperwork instead of prospects. Document and SOP drafting (Notion AI, ~$10/mo add-on, or the assistant you have; skip the add-on if you write two documents a month). Full agent platforms that promise the whole inbox (Lindy, ~$99/mo+): skip at 1–10 staff until the simple pieces above are habits; the vendor's 8–15 hours/week claims are the demo talking, and Chapter 10's probation applies to any tool making them. The measured claim, in your arithmetic: take your two audit numbers, halve them pessimistically, and price the checking ritual honestly into the tool's cost.

If minutes-saved times your hour doesn't clear that all-in cost by double, don't buy. A year-two illustration with round numbers, not a promise: say the audit finds meeting notes eating 120 minutes a week. Halve it pessimistically: 60 minutes. If you price your hour at $60, that's about $240 a month of time against Otter Pro's annual prepayment of roughly $100 (about $8.33 a month before the same-day skim, a couple of minutes per meeting, call it $10 a month of your time). The arithmetic clears by a mile, but only a completed first year, a clean current audit, and a tested exit clear the prepayment. Same math on a $99 agent platform against an honest 40 minutes a week saved: roughly $160 of time returned.

A whole-inbox agent needs closer watching than a receipt pile, so its check is a twenty-minute weekly run-check, not the monthly skim a narrow tool earns: another ~$80 a month of your time at the illustration's $60 figure, and the honest all-in cost is $179 against $160 returned. It doesn't clear at all, let alone by double. That is the formula's third part doing its job, and the platform waits. Your numbers will differ; the formula is the point. And the audit is yours to keep either way, because knowing where the evenings go is worth the fifteen minutes. The take-backs, named Anything that lands in a filing. Categorization is delegable; tax positions are not. The machine sorts; your accountant (or your carefully checked filing software, unchanged by this book) decides.

A wrong number in a tax filing is Chapter 1's "very bad spring," and the interpreting-rules row of the failure map lives right here. The machine's honest job at filing time is assembly: clean books, organized documents, a list of questions for the professional. Recordings of other people. A meeting transcript is other people's words in a third party's cloud. Before any notetaker joins a call: ask and get the yes, and check where recordings live and whether they train models. The fence covers your own crew too: a staff meeting is other people's words as much as a client call is, and some states require notice to employees before electronic monitoring, so the heads-up and the policy page apply inside the shop as much as out.

The category's biggest name shows why you check: Otter's own documentation (Aug 2026) says its standard service may use de-identified audio and transcripts to improve its AI, enterprise plans are opted out of that training by default while other plans are not, and deleting a conversation removes it from storage with no promise the models unlearn it (vendor-reported, plan-specific; your exact plan's current pages rule). Client calls under confidentiality (bookkeepers, advisors, health-adjacent trades): if a confidentiality agreement or a professional code binds you, don't record, full stop, until Chapter 12's policy page is in place. When in doubt: notes typed after the call are slower and completely yours. Payment execution. Drafting the invoice: machine. Chasing the overdue invoice with a polite note: machine, under the Chapter 6 rules.

Moving money (paying bills, issuing refunds, changing banking details): never, and not because today's tools ask to; the fence exists before the request does. Anything touching where money actually moves is a survivability fail by definition. The monthly skim itself. The one back-office task you never delegate is the checking of the delegations. Twenty minutes, coffee, once a month. It is the entire difference between books you supervise and books you hope about. Do this Friday About 40 minutes, $0 today. Run the audit (15 min): five buckets, honest minutes, circle the top two. Pick the matching workhorse (one, not both): meetings → Fathom or Otter free tier; receipts → the capture feature inside the accounting tool you already pay for.

If your exact plan does not include receipt capture, check the vendor's current feature page before signing up or uploading financial records; this book does not establish that Wave's free core includes it. Set it up and run it once on synthetic receipts or a meeting with only yourself unless Chapter 12 has cleared the exact tool, plan, account, data, permissions, storage, retention, and incident process. After clearance, one week's real receipts or one consented meeting may run. Do the check the same day: skim the summary, or verify approved receipt mappings and place every ambiguity in the exception queue. Calendar the monthly skim. Third Friday, 20 minutes, standing. Write "stay able to check" on the calendar entry; that's the whole job description.

If any recorded call or meeting has someone else in it (client or not): use the informed-consent script above, record the yes outside the recording, and park the tool until you've read its data page. No answer, hesitation, pressured staff agreement, or uncertainty about the local rule means typed notes instead. Two minutes that keep Chapter 12 short. The takeaway: the back office is floor-work with the source of truth in the room — delegate the capture, approved mappings, drafts, and (after an affirmative yes) the notes under fast checks; never ambiguous classifications, filings, money movement, or the monthly skim that keeps you able to catch a wrong number.

Anything that lands in a filing.
Categorization is delegable; tax positions are not.

Do this Friday
About 40 minutes, $0 today.

(An illustration, not a measurement; your Friday count will be the real number.) The chapters before this one hired specialists: a phone answerer, a marketing drafter, a notetaker. This chapter hires the two generalists that make the specialists worth having: an assistant (the do-anything desk worker you brief) and automation (the courier that moves facts between your systems so your hands don't).

They are different species with different failure shapes, and confusing them is how owners end up with $200 of point tools doing what $20 covers. After this chapter, you can: Decide assistant-versus-point-tool for any task with one question Kill your worst retype with one two-step automation on a free tier Run the free-tier math (Zapier vs Make) before the first paid automation dollar Hold the two automation fences: customer sends watched for their first month (then only the lowest-stakes class runs alone), and money never touched at all The assistant decision: one desk worker before any specialist Nearly everything Chapters 5 through 7 delegate (drafts, replies, summaries, follow-ups, documents) can be done, unglamorously, inside one general assistant subscription.

ChatGPT (free; Plus $20/mo; Pro tiers at $100 and $200/mo with different usage allowances), Claude (free tier; Pro $20/mo; Max from $100/mo), Gemini (free; paid tiers roughly $10–30/mo, secondary-sourced), Microsoft Copilot (Pro $20/mo; the M365 version adds $30/user/mo and only shines inside Office). OpenAI and Anthropic prices per their official pages as read Aug 2026; price, tax, availability, and allowances vary by region and plan and they change, so the dated official page rules. The arithmetic that matters: one $20/mo assistant, briefed with your Voice Pack and facts sheets, replaces the drafting layer of several $30–80/mo point tools. The point tool earns its keep only where it adds something the assistant can't: the phone actually being answered (Chapter 4), the receipt actually entering the books (Chapter 7), the post actually publishing on schedule.

Draft in the assistant; buy plumbing, not prose. Ask one question of any tool on your card: does it do anything besides draft? If no, mark it as a consolidation candidate, not an instant cancellation: compare quality, checking time, controls, data terms, collaboration/history, and total cost in a short probation, then use Chapter 13's tested-export and dependency gate. If yes, price the plumbing on its own merits. Pick by where you already live: Copilot if your business runs on Office, Gemini if it runs on Gmail and Docs, ChatGPT or Claude otherwise. The differences at owner-scale tasks are smaller than any vendor page implies. And Chapter 3's exit question (how do I get out?) gets perhaps the happiest answer in this category: switching assistants costs roughly a copy-paste of your Pack for a solo owner; with staff briefed on the tool, budget an afternoon of retraining too.

Hold the subscription loosely, and follow Chapter 3's month-to-month rule for the first year. Set the two defaults before the first real task; they are this book's standing data fence, applied to assistants. First, the training controls: three vendors used default-on consumer training when checked, while Claude used a consent screen whose improvement toggle was preselected on; Copilot's consumer default came from Microsoft's August 2024 announcement, with business plans excluded. The retained record for Claude and Copilot still relies partly on secondary or relayed confirmation because their live privacy pages could not be opened in this research environment, so confirm the dated control name and desired OFF state in Chapter 12 and on the current vendor page before any real task. Second, the rule that client-identifying data stays out of consumer tiers: the fence is on pasting lists, records, and files, and trimming a surname is not anonymizing: a first name plus a role, a location, an event, or a quoted line can still identify someone. For live client data, a privacy notice or engagement-letter disclosure is one check, not permission by itself. Chapter 12 must first clear the minimum fields, lawful authority or consent, vendor agreement or processing terms, subprocessors, storage and transfers, security and access, retention and deletion, incident process, and jurisdiction-specific advice when uncertain. Automation tools watch for a trigger (new form entry, new booking, missed call) and perform steps (add the row, send the text, create the invoice draft). The learning curve is steeper, and mind the unit: a credit is one step, not one finished job, so a five-step scenario spends five credits per run. The honest free-tier math is mechanical, not demographic: Zapier allows 100 tasks a month and two steps, while Make lists 1,000 credits and two active scenarios; one five-step run spends five Make credits. Estimate your own runs, steps, and required integrations against both current pricing pages before choosing.

Worked once so the shape is concrete: the booking-confirmation email is the trigger; "add a row to the jobs sheet" is the action.

Run the first ten real events in shadow or draft mode, where the automation cannot mutate the live system or message a customer. Only after those ten land cleanly does the narrow action go live.

Automation does not confabulate; it repeats: a person who mis-enters one booking mis-enters one booking; a misconfigured automation mis-enters every booking, identically, at 3 a.m. The check that fits the shape is a weekly look at every run since last time, confirming the fields landed where they should and every failure raised its alert; Chapter 7's monthly skim inherits the automations as one more line. The measured claim, yours: your Friday retype count × thirty seconds (or your own timed number) × your hourly figure, against $0 to Make-Core money. Most single retypes clear trivially or fail honestly; the count decides, not the demo. Build versus buy at your size The internet is full of owners building custom AI platforms, agent swarms, four Mac Minis in a closet.

One mid-size account in this book's research, a founder's own telling through a local news segment: Growbo, a marketing agency, built a custom human-plus-AI platform and reports 700+ hours and $12,000 saved in four months with revenue up (Spectrum Bay News 9, Apr 2025; figures self-reported by the founder). The take-backs, named Automated sends to customers, month one.

Any automation whose last step messages a real customer runs in draft-mode first (it prepares, you send) until a month of run-watching has shown you its shape. After that, only a frozen, human-approved lowest-stakes template with approved field substitution may run alone. Generated or paraphrased customer wording remains draft-only. (Chapter 6's rule, now as plumbing; and a sent message is a regulated message, so the consent and opt-out lanes Chapter 6 names, TCPA in the US and CASL in Canada, ride along no matter which courier fires it.) Anything that moves money. No automation touches payments, refunds, payroll, or banking details. Not "carefully." Not at all. (Drafting and sending an invoice or a payment link is paperwork, not payment, and stays allowed under the sends fence; the line is anything that debits, charges, refunds, or changes where money goes without a human's click.)

The blast radius fails the survivability question by definition (Chapter 7's fence, extended to the couriers). Building your own platform. Until the day your business is a software business, buying beats building; revisit annually, not after each impressive demo. The consolidation migration. "Replace your five tools with our one platform" is oversold at your size (the all-in-one savings mostly accrue to 1–4 person teams on the simplest stacks, per the category research, and best-of-breed plus glue usually wins). Moving systems costs a quarter; let the glue connect what already works before any tool's sales page convinces you to move house. Do this Friday About 45 minutes at the desk, plus the tally riding along all day. $0. Friday designs and schedules the build; the first connected setup gets its own 60–90 minute block because the tests and rollback proof are part of the work.

Count the retypes for one workday: a tally mark every time the same fact enters a second system by hand. Circle the biggest repeat offender. Make the assistant decision with the arithmetic above: list your point-tool subscriptions that only draft (words, posts, replies); mark any the $20 assistant plus your Pack already covers; queue the redundant ones for Chapter 13's audit. Sketch one two-step automation without connecting live data: name the trigger, action, authoritative source, minimum permissions, owner, alert, manual fallback, rollback, and the normal, duplicate, missing-field, malformed, and retry tests it must pass. Calendar a 60–90 minute setup block to build and run those fake-record tests, followed by at least ten clean shadow events across the predeclared observation window.

Live mutation waits until the tests, clean-event count, and window all pass; review every run and alert weekly for four weeks after promotion. Write the two fences at the top of your notes: "Nothing generated sends to customers. After a watched month, only frozen approved templates with approved fields may send alone. Nothing touches money, ever." Then flip the assistant training controls this chapter names, confirm the desired OFF state, and keep client lists out of consumer tiers. The takeaway: one briefed assistant covers your drafting layer for $20 before any point tool earns a dollar, and automation is a courier that repeats — glue your systems one proven retype at a time, watch the runs, and keep it away from sends you haven't proven and money entirely.

chunks.text: Chapter 9 Your Trade's Own Traps Every trade eventually hears about the tool "built for us": the plumber hears about dispatch platforms, the restaurant hears about AI phone orders, the salon hears about the booking receptionist, the bookkeeper hears about the AI that does bookkeeping. The pitch is always the same and always true as far as it goes: a vertical tool arrives pre-trained in your trade's vocabulary. It knows what a re-pipe is, what a no-show costs, what a covers count means. This chapter is about when that's worth paying for, and about the two traps that come folded inside the fit: dirty data feeding it, and the supervision that fades once it fits. Tony Naser owns Crush Pizza in Massachusetts and Mickey's N.Y. Pizza in New Hampshire, and, since 2024, an AI has answered his phones and taken orders, handling over a thousand calls a month per store by his own estimate.

He employs more people than before, by his own count. His vendor claims big numbers for the category (98.6% accuracy, phone revenue up 26%), and those are the vendor's numbers, so grade them like every vendor number in this book (start by assuming the true figures are worse, and notice neither number is what anchors this chapter). What makes his story the anchor of this chapter is that one independent report (Boston Globe, Jan 18 2026, with its Jan 22 update) carries all three layers at once. The win above is layer one. Layer two is the failure: a customer named Jillian Kent, stuck "in a loop with an automated program" across two locations and a second day, over a $14 missing salad. Another customer's refund had been requested but not received at the follow-up. Layer three is the quiet one, the second of those traps. The reporting found owners monitoring less as the AI bedded in.

One operator, Nick's Place, twelve stores (well past this book's 1–10 band, but instructive), told the Globe he "worries less about what's going on in his stores" and went home early on Halloween. His line about the AI: he looks at it "like I'm paying an employee, but it's also cheaper than an employee." Hold that sentence against everything since Chapter 1. Cheaper than an employee, supervised less than an employee, and answering your customers by name. The deeper trap is not that the tools are bad. It is that fit breeds trust, and trust is how the checks stop. What the two questions say about verticals Chapter 1's screen for any delegation (can you check it at a glance, and could you survive the worst version?) has a vertical-specific answer. Glance-checkable?

Better than horizontal tools, usually: the vertical's output lands in your own operational world (a booked job, a placed order, a filled slot), where you have Chapter 1's fastest checks.
